speechtext:
Right .Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, hon. members will have learned with deep regret of the death, last night, of the member for Kent, Ontario, Doctor James W. Rutherford.
While death, when it occurs, seems to take us by surprise, in the case of Doctor Rutherford, the surprise is that having met with the very serious accident he did, in September, 1935, he continued to live as long as he did. Only a very brave and resolute spirit could have endured the physical suffering he endured for so long a time and have risen above it to the extent that on occasions he did. Death to the doctor meant release from suffering borne with the utmost patience and fortitude over three and a half years.
The personnel of the House of Commons has so largely changed in recent years that I doubt if there are, in its membership at the present time, one-fifth of those who were members of parliament at the time Doctor Rutherford himself became a member in 1926. The accident with which the Doctor met occurred in the course of the electoral campaign of 1935. It deprived him of further personal participation in the elections, and deprived him also of the opportunity of taking his seat in the present parliament, save on one occasion when, during the last session, he made an appearance in a wheel chair for a day or two in this house.
Many hon. members, therefore, will have had little or no acquaintance with Doctor Rutherford, and will be unable to appreciate, as those of us who knew him in the years he sat in the Commons between 1926 and 1935, how great is the loss suffered by the constituency he represented, by the public life of our country, and by his profession because of the injuries which brought prematurely to its close a career which had already been marked by many achievements, and gave promise of long continued personal and public service.
Doctor Rutherford's life associations were with the western portion of the province of Ontario and more immediately with the county of Kent in which he was born in 1875, and with the city of Chatham at whose public schools and collegiate institute, he received his early education, and where the greater part of his life was spent. He was a graduate of the university of Toronto. He pursued postgraduate studies in medicine at University College, London, England. Doctor Rutherford soon came to be recognized as a leading physician and surgeon in western Ontario, and at the time of his membership in this house was looked upon as one of the leading surgeons in our country. In the choice of his profession, Doctor Rutherford followed and was, no doubt, inspired by the example of his ' father who, for half a century, had practised medicine in Chatham.
The Late J. W. Rutherford

Doctor Rutherford's popularity in the county of Kent was evidenced by his selection as one of the candidates in the general election of 1925, by his election to parliament in 1926, and his re-election at the general elections of 1930 and 1935.
Recalling the part which he took in the proceedings of this house in the two preceding parliaments, and the position he had come to occupy in his profession, I can only express the regret which I know will be shared by all, that one whose life was so wholly devoted to the well-being of others, so eminently useful and skilful, should have been brought to its close in circumstances so tragic.
Doctor Rutherford's loss will be particularly felt by the Liberal party of which, in the province of Ontario, he was recognized as a foremost member. In his passing the government suffers the loss of one of its ablest supporters, and many of us, the loss of one who was the most loyal and devoted of friends.
The sympathy of hon. members will go out, in full measure, to Mrs. Rutherford and to her son and daughter who, during the past three and a half years, have suffered so much in the way of anxiety and have now lost to sight the one who throughout their lives had been the centre of their affections.
We may look, I know, to His Honour the Speaker to convey to Mrs. Rutherford and the others who have been so greatly bereaved, the expression of our deepest sympathy.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I join with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in expressing to the family of the late Doctor Rutherford, the sympathy of our party. Whenever on these painful occasions one rises to pay tribute to some member who has gone, unconsciously a thought as to the high mortality rate of the House of Commons comes to one's mind. Only a few weeks ago we were speaking about the deaths of David Beaubier and Samuel Jacobs, one from each side of the house, and Doctor Rutherford is the third member whose loss we mourn in this early part of the session.
Naturally, I did not have the opportunity of knowing Doctor Rutherford as intimately as my right hon. friend and the party opposite, but the little I did know of him was to his credit. Like the late David Beaubier, of whom I spoke a few weeks ago, he did not take part in debate in the house as frequently as some of the rest of us. But I have often wondered if perhaps those of us who speak so frequently render as much service as those who speak less. Doctor Rutherford certainly bore a good reputation as a member of the

various committees upon which he served, and as one who looked after the interests of his constituents and carried out whatever other duties devolved upon him as a member of the House of Commons.
If I may be permitted to say so, many times in the house I have been struck with the fact that men who originally have been trained as medical practitioners have given valuable service in the House of Commons.
I have come to the conclusion that a medical training affords a splendid mental development for the work of the house. Doctor Rutherford was certainly no exception in that respect; he always gave the service expected of him.
I should like to join sincerely indeed with my right hon. friend and the party to which he belongs in expressing sympathy to that party upon its loss of another outstanding member, and I would join with him and other hon. members of the house in passing on, through you, Mr. Speaker, to the family of Doctor Rutherford, our deep sympathy.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, hon. members in the group to which I belong would like to join with the others in expressing through you our sympathy to Mrs. Rutherford and the family in the loss which they have sustained.

Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as hon. members in this group had no opportunity of knowing Doctor Rutherford, except by report and from the one day during which he so bravely sat in the house and showed he was able to endure suffering with calmness and fortitude, it seems to me it is fitting that we should associate ourselves with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in his eloquent and fitting tribute. We desire, sir, that you remember us when you extend to the bereaved family the consolations of the house.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temiscouata): Mr. Speaker, Doctor James Warren Rutherford was one of the most adroit and the most skilful surgeons not only of the province of Ontario but of the whole of Canada. He had a large practice, and his career as a practitioner was very brilliant. He performed so many operations which were considered as miracles in modern surgery that his name was respected and honoured by the heads of the medical profession on the whole north American continent.
It was at first a great sacrifice for him to enter into politics. Until then he had given all his time to his numerous patients, who were so dear to him. But he was a man of deep convictions. He was a true Canadian of Scotch ancestry, and a Liberal at heart.

Civil Service-Superannuation Act
He was a strong believer in the necessity of promoting Liberal ideals and Liberal policies for the welfare of his fellow countrymen. From 1926 to 1935 he divided his time between attending to his large practice and attending to the sittings of the House of Commons. His colleagues who had the privilege of knowing him intimately during that period will always cherish the most pleasant memory of his kindness, of his discreet humour, of his wisdom, and of his everlasting friendship.
While campaigning in the last general election he was the victim of an unfortunate accident. He was in the hospital, for the first time as a patient, when he learned that he had again been elected by a large majority. Then the suggestion was made to him to resign his seat in favour of some one else. He refused, saying that death only could break the happy association with parliament, which he prized so much. Last year he came to the house on a wheel chair, to attend a debate in which he was particularly interested.
If I may be permitted to add a few personal recollections, I would say that it was he who invited me to speak, for the first time outside of Ottawa, in Ontario. The occasion was in April, 1932, at the annual meeting of the Ontario Women's Liberal Association, which was held in his city, the beautiful maple city of Chatham. Mr. Hepburn spoke on that occasion. On the following day, in company with another dear friend of ours, Mr. Melville Rossie, editor of the London Advertiser, we went to speak at Lucan, where our friend from Middlesex East, Colonel Ross, also spoke. At that time Mr. Hepburn was apparently in very good health. I attended another meeting at Chatham on June 14, 1934, which was held in the armouries. On that occasion the hall was packed to capacity, and the two most prominent people in attendance were Mr. Hepburn and Doctor Rutherford who, in the meantime, had saved Mr. Hepburn's life. Mr. Hepburn will tell anyone that the fact he is still alive is due to the skilful operation performed by Doctor Rutherford.
I should like therefore to join with others who have spoken and to express my deep grief at the death of such a dear friend, one who was a great medical man, a great Liberal and a great Scotsman.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) a question with regard to the provisions of the trade agreement with the United States. speakeroldname: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-ALLOCATION OF CATTLE QUOTAS
speechtext:
As I stated during the
debate on the resolution with regard to the trade agreement with the United States, negotiations were in progress between this government and the government of the United States in connection with the allocation of the quota on heavy cattle. Those negotiations were carried on by an official of the Department of Trade and Commerce

Canada-Germany-Shipments
and an official of the department of Agriculture. At the time I spoke on the matter an arrangement had been arrived at, but I was not in position then to make a statement. However, to-day I can say that the President of the United States has signed a proclamation allocating among countries of export the quantity of cattle weighing 700 pounds or more each, other than cows imported psecially for dairy purposes, entitled to enter the United States during the remainder of the year 1939 at the reduced duty of 1J cents per pound provided for in the trade agreement.
In accordance with the provisions of the trade agreement the government of Canada officially requested the government of the United States of America to allocate the quotas on this type of cattle for the remainder of this calendar year. Article III of the trade agreement provides that the share allocated to Canada shall be based upon the proportion of the total imports supplied by Canada in past years, account being taken in so far as practicable in appropriate cases of any special factors which may have affected or may be affecting the trade in the article in question. After carefully considering all the factors and after consultation with the government of Canada, the president decided that imports during the years 1936 and 1937 are representative of imports of this class of cattle. Accordingly, the allocation for the remainder of the year 1939 is made on the basis of imports during the above years. This will give Canada 86-2 per cent of the quota and other countries 13-8 per cent. This means that the share of the quarterly quotas of 60,000 head allocated to Canada is 51,720 head. The allocation of the annual quota for the remainder of this year will be based on 225,000 head less the 60,000 head imported during the first quarter of the year, or a total of 165,000 head, of which the share allocated to Canada will amount to 142,230 head.

purposes of clarity I might make a reference to the payments agreement to which my hon. friend (Mr. Reid) referred.
When the payments agreement, which was complementary to the trade agreement made with Germany in 1936, was concluded, the vital principle of it was that the German government obligated itself to provide exchange for the purchase of Canadian goods at least to the amount of all purchases made by Canada in Germany.
The government had its attention directed to a complaint that certain United States commodities, in this case dried apples, were imported into Canada in transit and reexported to Germany, and the fear was that the amount of the shipment in money value would be charged against the amount of exchange that would be allocated for the purchase of Canadian goods. Accordingly, representations have been made through the Canadian government's trade commissioner at Berlin to the German authorities asking that payment for shipment of dried apples exported from Canada to Germany be not made from the funds accruing under the German-Cana-dian payments agreement unless the shipments carried a Canadian inspection certificate. At present they are not very numerous and not very popular in Canada, but they can qualify for membership in the leadership league, and with such fine motives and high ideals as must be adopted with such a leader they will have an opportunity to propagate their specious thoughts.
What has this government done in the way of increasing trade? I have said before that our economic ills can be, if not entirely at any. rate immeasurably, lightened in this day and generation by one method only, and that is trade. I take no stock in the theories of the Social Credit group. Whatever merit they have, if any, cannot be applied in the trade

world of to-day. They have to convert the world to their thoughts and they are not making very much headway in their own province of Alberta. The Commonwealth Cooperative Federation lightly dismiss the question of trade, but they will not dare vote against this resolution,. The theory of national socialism is having a real trial in Germany and Italy and with so many rugged individualists in the party on the other side I am quite satisfied that in their hearts they know and recognize the value of trading, but they carefully restrain their'enthusiasm; for that would mean giving credit to the government, which is not in -their lexicon.
And now we come to the Tories. It is said that there is no difference between the Liberals and the Tories on tariffs. I humbly suggest that those who say so can hardly do so now with any degree of truth. That slogan is like the other one of which I spoke-if it is not dead it is certainly damned. There is evidence of that. In the year 1936 after the trade treaty came into effect there were reductions on 192 items and in 1937 there were reductions on 354. Surely that is a fair record. Going further, however, I find that not only has the government reduced the tariff rate on a great variety of items, but it has also transferred an appreciable number to the free list. Evidence of this is seen in the import figures for the fiscal year 1937-38, when out of a total of $799,069,000 worth of goods imported into Canada, $364,904,000 worth entered duty free; that is, 45 per cent of all the goods which entered Canada during the last fiscal year came in without having to pay duty.
My time is going fast and I must hurry to a conclusion, but I wish to deal with some things which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) has said. Some speakers have taken the position that to aver that these treaties have any bearing on the peace of the world is far-fetched. The leader of the opposition, on pages 1051 and 1056 of Hansard, devoted two columns to ridiculing this, and on page 1053 he said:
I submit that the talk about this treaty as having anything whatever to do with world peace is simply what Mr. Oliver Stanley called it, " eyewash."
It is a pity that the leader of the opposition in the exuberance of his verbosity should utter such sentiments. In his position as leader of the opposition he is inclined to put the emphasis on the opposition and forget the leadership. I suggest that he should cultivate the virtues of understatement. He quoted with approval what Mr. Stanley said. Let me quote a greater authority. I have
here a little book entitled Together We Stand, written by Leonard J. Reid, financial editor of the London Daily Telegraph, with a foreword by Viscount Horne, a former chancellor of the exchequer. This book tells of Mr. Reid's visit to the United States in 1937 and deals with trade relations and the psychology of the two peoples. It is quite apposite and apropos of this particular discussion. Referring to Mr. Reid, Viscount Horne says in the foreword:
No more confident observer could have applied his mind to the problems of the present relations between America and Great Britain; and none could have obtained more adequate information. He has formed certain very definite impressions which he records in this book. It is interesting to observe, from statements in the public press, that Sir Josiah Stamp, who has newly returned from a tour in the United States of America, has arrived at conclusions practically identical in character with those disclosed in this treatise.
An on the second page of the foreword he
says:
A large section of American opinion has come to the conclusion that the prosperity of the United States depends in a considerable measure upon the extension of international trade, and the present administration is seeking means by which such trade can be fostered. The Secretary of State, Mr. Cordell Hull, is an ardent champion of this policy, and he is ably seconded by Mr. Wallace, who has preached with great persistency and unabated enthusiasm that the success of farming in the United States must depend upon the availability of export markets.
The leader of the opposition says that to talk of peace in connection with this agreement is "eyewash."

Yes, but my hon. friend approved it. At page 28 Mr. Reid says:
The government and the leaders of the business world in the United States, under the courageous lead and inspiration of Mr. Cordell Hull, the secretary of state, are now convinced that America's old economic policy of prohibitive tariffs and isolation was wrong and harmful both to herself and to the world. Having come to this conclusion, Mr. Hull, who has been working for years at the successful arrangement of bilateral trade treaties, now wishes to arrange one with Britain. His belief is that freer conditions of world trade must be established if the world is to escape another catastrophic depression and probably another world war. America, he and his followers believe, cannot lead the way to this goal alone. America and Britain or, better still, America and the British commonwealth, working in cooperation, could do so.
I may interject that this was written in 1937.
They see the world, as it is at present, drifting inevitably into chaos, and envisage a British-American trade pact, opening up the door to a series of agreements on currency, gold and a host of other matters, as the only

alternative to rapidly approaching world disaster. So they sincerely and honestly want it very much.
These are the observations of the financial editor of the Daily Telegraph on his return to London, speaking of the viewpoint of the Americas. Then on pages 79 and 80 of the same book he says:
It is firmly believed in official circles at Washington that a series of agreements between the United States and Britain, designed to free and encourage international trade and to stabilize the currency position, would be rapidly and eagerly followed by Scandinavia and the whole of what is known as the "sterling bloc," and also by all the countries of South America. The picture thus presented is one of such a huge portion of the earth's surface working together with a common aim of increasing trade and prosperity and providing security against financial shocks, that, in the Washington view, there is no nation in the world which could afford to defy it or even stand outside it.
Then, in answer to the leader of the opposition in regard to " eyewash," he goes on to say:
This is the big idealistic vision which is in vogue in Washington to-day. The very bigness of the conception causes cynics to write it off as a mere vague and unpractical philosophy. But any English statesman-
And, I would interject, any Canadian statesman.
-who decided that minor difficulties of tariff schedules were of more importance than the attempt to achieve, with real practical hopes of success, a new basis for prosperity and security in the world, would surely be risking the direct condemnation of history.
Those are the words of a distinguished visitor to the United States, words which have been quoted with approval by Viscount Home, a former chancellor of the exchequer.

Canada is a member of the British commonwealth, bound up equally with ourselves and her fellow dominions with the whole Ottawa system of exclusive preferences, yet Canada has managed to devise and put into practice a trade treaty with the United States. It took a lot of time to devise, a great deal of hard work and a very great deal of good will. The negotiators started in a small way, facing hosts of difficulties and ironing them out slowdy and patiently until to-day the American-Canadian pact is working smoothly to the mutual advantage of both countries and is definitely increasing the volume of trade. In the ease of Canada itself it is not surprising that the maximum good will for the project of agreement with America should be forthcoming. Not merely geographical propinquity, but the interweaving of trade interests naturally makes it of vital importance for Canada to be on the best possible terms in every way with her great and powerful neighbour.
Then on page 65:
Finally, to those who say that the Ottawa agreements obstruct the project of British-American trade cooperation, I would reply that the difficulties in the way of a trade agreement between Britain and America, or between America and most of the British Empire are less difficult in their technicalities than was the agreement between Canada and America whose economic situations and needs have a greater similarity than that which exists between America and England.
So we have the evidence of this distinguished Englishman, Mr. Speaker, and the sure and certain knowledge that this government and this nation are entitled to take credit not only for making the first breach in the wall of economic nationalism but also for preparing the way for the completion of the agreement between the United Kingdom and the United States of America.
In this book Mr. Reid refers to a publication issued by the National Foreign Trade Council of the United States, which states much better than I could exactly what trade treaties mean and why those of us on this-side of the house are so glad to support them. At page 33, under the heading "Foreign trade and the domestic welfare" and the subheading "The choice that confronts us," the foreign trade council gives these alternatives:
With Increasing Foreign Trade
A higher standard of living.
A self-reliant agriculture.
Full employment in industry.
"Payment in full" for our exports.
A free and unregimented economy.
Sound money.
The road to international concord.
With Foreign Trade Restricted
A lower standard of living.
Continued agricultural subsidies.
Permanent large unemployment.
Closing the door to payment for exports.
Regimentation of agriculture and industry.
Currency tinkering.
The threat of military conflict.

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
So far as we in the west are concerned I think I can quote the words that were contained in a letter I received the other day from one of my constituents. This man, who is a Ukrainian, said: "We do not want any Christmas gifts in the form of bonuses. Give us a chance to trade and to buy our goods in freer, lower-priced markets, and we will look after ourselves." This is the viewpoint of most of us in the west. We do not want any Christmas gifts by way of bonuses but we do want to purchase our goods in freer, lower-priced markets. This treaty, together with the 1935 treaty, will go a long way towards acceding to that request. Mine is a rural constituency, and naturally my first sympathies are with my people and their problems. It is a mixed constituency, with a large Ukrainian population, who have created a settlement which, from a farming point of view, could not be bettered. In 1935 I asked my constituents to support me as a member of the Liberal party, in order that we might have in power a government that would reduce these barriers to trade. I can go back to them now and say, "What I told you during the campaign is being carried into effect by this government to-day. They have made the greatest reductions in the tariff of this ' country to be made by any government in Canada." I know they are going forward to ever-increasing markets, and in that way they will lessen the burden of our producers. I say also that there is only one party in Canada to which we can look for that freedom of trade, and that, I am glad to say, is the party I support to-day.
Mr. KARL K. HOMUTH (Waterloo South):	Mr. Speaker, in rising to protest
against the adoption of this motion for approval of the trade treaty I wish also to protest in the house against the unwarranted and continual castigations of people engaged in industry in eastern Canada. I happen to be engaged in industry, and very much interested in the development and prosperity of industry in Canada. I realize the best customer industry in this country can have is the prosperous agriculturist. But so, too, the best customer the agriculturist can have in Canada is the prosperous working man in the factories throughout the dominion.
I have listened attentively to the speeches of the ministers and of hon. members opposite. I have listened carefully to what they had to say. One after the other got up and criticized industry; not one member opposite has stood in his place in the house and had a kind word to say for industry in Canada or those engaged in it.
I wonder what the members from that great industrial area of Windsor are going to do in connection with this trade treaty?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: They will be like a clam.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: I wonder what the Liberal members from Brantford, Toronto, Renfrew, Oshawa and other industrial areas of Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes are going to do?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: You will hear the member from Windsor.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: What are they going to do with this trade agreement?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: They are all satisfied with the treaty, and they are not taking up the time of the house.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
The fact of the matter is that they are not satisfied with the trade agreement. The fact is that they will support the trade agreement in the meantime, but I should not be a bit surprised if, when the various items come up for discussion, one after the other they will stand in their places and try to satisfy their own districts, and register their protests against some of the things that are being done in the treaty.
This continual tariff changing by the government, as I have said before in the house, is doing nothing but giving industry the jitters, and it is slowly but surely lowering the standard of living of the industrial workers of Canada. Member after member, particularly those from the western provinces, have stood in the house and demanded protection for the western wheat farmer. I have never known of a bill presented to the house to do something for western Canada to which eastern members have taken exception. In those terrible days of the last few years eastern Canada unhesitatingly went to the assistance of western Canada in every possible way. I have said before and I repeat that if we are to solve the problems of Canada there can be no east, no west, no Ontario, no Quebec

we have to look at these matters from the broad Canadian viewpoint.
So I say I resent very much hon. members standing in the house and continually taking a lot of fun out of criticizing the so-called industrial leaders in the eastern part of this country. During all my political life I have fought, and will continue to fight, for the industrial workers and the farmers. I come from a county which is prominent not only industrially but also from the standpoint of agriculture. Perhaps in no place in Canada is there better exemplification of the extent to which the rural producer and the urban industrial worker depend on each other for
1394	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
their prosperity. For the few moments at my disposal, therefore, I shall deal with the matter of agriculture.
Sitting in the house and time and again listening to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) deal with matters pertaining to agriculture, about the only thing I have heard him discuss has been the question of wheat. So far he has said nothing with regard to vegetable growers, fruit growers and people engaged in various other forms of agriculture, particularly the forms common in eastern Canada. From what is happening in Canada to-day I can see very plainly that when the minister deals with wheat, apparently he is not very much interested in the wheat grower of eastern Canada.
In 1938 there was a carry-over of eight or ten million bushels of eastern wheat. In the same year we produced eighteen or twenty million bushels. Therefore we have a tremendous carry-over of wheat, and yet to-day throughout eastern Canada, and particularly in Ontario, hundreds of thousands of bushels of subsidized United States wheat are coming into this country and are being milled in Ontario. On Saturday last the wheat quotation to a Canadian mill in Buffalo was 46 cents, and the quotation to a United States mill in that city was 72 cents. Yesterday there was a spread of 30 cents a bushel between the price of wheat in Buffalo for the United States mill and the price of wheat in that city for the Canadian mill. That is the wheat which is coming into this country, a country flooded with wheat. We do not know what to do with it.
Hours and days of the time of the house have been taken up in an effort to find a solution of our wheat problem. Yet here are these thousands of bushels coming into Canada to be milled, while the farmers of Ontario who buy their bread are sitting at the table and eating bread made from subsidized United States wheat, at a time when their granaries are full of their own wheat, and they do not know what to do with it. Surely the time has come when something must be done for the wheat farmer of eastern Canada. I say in all seriousness that I trust the governments of Ontario and Quebec, if they do not already know it, will take cognizance of what is going on, and will protest and urge that the federal government is absolutely neglecting the wheat farmer of eastern Canada.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: What did you do between 1930 and 1935?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Answer that first.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I don't care what was done in 1930 or 1935. What I am concerned about is the welfare of the people of Canada. We are not looking back; we are looking forward. And if this government would look forward, as we are trying to do, it would not attempt to put through a trade treaty such as this.
Much has been said regarding the great benefits which will accrue to agriculture throughout Canada. I was not only interested but well pleased when from his place in the house this afternoon the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) told us the government had made arrangements with the government of the United States whereby our portion of the quota on cattle could go into, the United States. I still maintain that the understanding given to the people of this country was that Canada was to receive one-hundred per cent of that 225,000 head. One does not need to go any further than Hansard and read the statement of the Minister of' Agriculture when the matter was brought up in the house by the hon. member for Haldi-mand (Mr. Senn). On page 822 of Hansard the minister is reported as follows:
I might add that there is a provision in the agreement whereby, if quotas work out as this one apparently has, through consultation with the United States government, an arrangement may be made with regard to it in order to make it work as it was intended to work.
There is no question that the Minister of Agriculture has admitted that the intent was, that we were to have 225,000 head.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: I do not want my hon.. friend putting words in my mouth. If he will read all the statement he will see that I said exactly the opposite.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: It is in Hansard. The minister may read it to-morrow.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: It is not in Hansard as the hon. member states. He should read the whole statement. The statement shows that we never at any time had the whole quota.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Do you deny the words "as it was intended to work"?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Read the whole statement. It is that Mexico always had part of it.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
The peculiar thing about this whole trade agreement is that whatever concessions we got from the United States are on a quota basis. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has referred to the fact that less than two per cent of the shoes purchased in Canada are imported. We might do the same thing and work out, not what could go into the United States but what can go in,

Canada-United. States Trade Agreement
We can send milk and cream into the United States only to the limit of the quota, but we impose no quota on goods coming into this country. Our tariff on wheat is 12 cents a bushel as compared with a duty of 42 cents on wheat going into the United States. This is the government with which they made an appeasement treaty. This is the government to which they looked with such great friendliness as to what was going to happen as a result of this trade agreement. What is happening as a result of this trade agreement? The farmers of eastern Canada are suffering because of the hundreds of thousands of bushels of wheat that are coming into this country.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: What is the quota on boots and shoes going into the United States?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: There is no quota on boots and shoes going into the United States, and the minister knows that only too well. I shall have something to say about shoes later on. What I want to emphasize is that those things which they point out to the farmers as being of such great benefit are on such a ridiculous quota basis. Even the increased number of cattle that we can send into the United States under this new agreement amounts to about one-third of one per cent of their total consumption. Other hon. members have already told this house what the milk quota means. The county of Waterloo is not a dairying county, but it produces three times as much milk as the total United States quota. We produce as much cream in that county as is provided for by the United States quota. The amount which we can send to the United States would give every American citizen three tablespoons of cream once a year. What a wonderful thing they have given to us! What a wonderful friendly gesture that is!

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
It saved
a world war, though.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Of course. My hon.
friend referred to the number of shoes coming into this country. I have said before, and I repeat, that the question is not the number of shoes that come into this country, but how many would come in if our shoe manufacturers did not lower wages and the quality of their product in order to compete against the cheap United States shoes. If it were not that I have some regard for the dignity of this house I would have brought some shoes here to show some of the westerners the type of shoe that they have been told will come in here cheaper and thus reduce the cost of their wearing apparel, production costs, and
so on. They are shoes for evening wear, ladies' shoes, and so on. I should like to see some of the western or eastern rural housewives wearing this type of shoe as they work around the barns.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: They have stopped working in the barns in the west.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
The same thing is true in connection with furniture. It is not a question of the amount of furniture that may come into this country; it is the threat of the furniture that may come in. Our furniture manufacturers must be prepared to make a product which will compete with the United States article. My hon. friends from the west laugh when we talk about protection for industry in Canada, but let them stand up in this house and say whether or not they have accepted the policy of protection. They have accepted the government bonus on wheat, which is protection in a different way. Then this year the Minister of Agriculture is offering them protection in still another way. Eastern Canada is not objecting to that. Eastern Canada is not saying that this should not be done for the west. But eastern Canada does say that you should have some regard for the great industrial areas in eastern Canada and for the industrial workers employed in the various industries in that part of the country. That is all we are asking. Is that not fair? If we would quit playing politics with our wheat policy and other matters and get down to business, we would be in a better position to solve our problems without all the bickering that is going on.
Last June and July the boot and shoe workers' union in South Waterloo protested to the government against the provisions of this treaty. Protests were also sent by the boot and shoe manufacturers. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has said that he received no protests from the shoe industry in his riding.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: That is quite correct.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
But the minister has received protests from boot and shoe manufacturers who represent the boot and shoe manufacturers in North Waterloo. It might be interesting to deal with some of these protests for a moment.
In June or July of 1938 the boot and shoe manufacturers' association came to Ottawa and placed before the government a bi-ief setting forth the condition of the shoe industry and how they were threatened with the importations from the United States. At about the same time many of the ministers were sent letters by the boot and shoe workers' union

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
of South Waterloo protesting against the conditions which obtained in the shoe industry. This letter was signed by Marvin McKenzie, secretary treasurer of the Canadian shoe workers' union. It reads:
Owing to the fact that we have a Conservative representative in our district since the death of the late A. M. Edwards, I as secretary of local three of above organization representing some 400 members have been instructed to call your attention to the great number of shoes being imported into Canada from the U.S.A. and the extremely low prices at which they are being offered to the public.
We feel that these shoes are being shipped into Canada at considerably lower prices than they can be produced and it is working a hardship on the manufacturers and the workers.
Our organization has many members out of work and so many working short time and this unfair competition is definitely making it so much worse.
The shoes in question particularly are ladies' cheap evening shoes.
We have been informed that some of the retailers have stated that they are not buying this class of footwear in Canada for next season.
In view of the foregoing conditions, we respectfully request you use every means available to investigate this menace with a view of helping the manufacturers to operate successfully and make it possible for the workers to retain their self-respect by keeping off relief.
We trust that you will give this your favourable consideration.
Yours respectfully,
The Canadian Shoe Workers' Union, Marvin McKenzie,
Secretary-Treasurer.
This is the letter that went from the secretary of the boot and shoe workers' union. Mr. F. It. Sims, for the commissioner of customs, replied that considerable effort would be involved in investigating the whole matter of costs and determining whether or not these shoes were being dumped into Canada.
The secretary of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) also replied to the boot and shoe workers' union, as follows:
Dear Sir,-
The Prime Minister has asked me to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of recent date, with respect to conditions in the shoe manufacturing business due to the importation of shoes from the United States.
Mr. King wishes me to let you know that the representations contained in your communication have been carefully noted.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) also received a letter from the boot and shoe workers' union, to which he replied:
Your letter of recent date addressed to the Minister of Labour has been received and will be brought to his attention at the first opportunity.

All this occurred in June and July of 1938, when the treaty was under consideration. Yet in spite of all these protests made to the minister and the government, the government went ahead and negotiated the trade treaty with the United States, which will result, when the excise duty is taken off, in reducing the protection on shoes made in Canada by nine to ten per cent

and this in spite of all the protests made by these various organizations representing the shoe industry and the workers engaged in that industry.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: What is the present rate of duty on shoes?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He can tell you. On January 23, 1939. a letter was received by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, reading as follows:
Dear Sir,-
You will shortly receive a letter which I have instructed our manager, Mr. Roy Weaver, to write to you in connection with the shoe industry. This letter is prompted by your remarks to the house that imports were less than two per cent of the Canadian consumption.
While this statement is quite true when one takes the general picture, the story is entirely different when one analyses the shoe trade in its various classifications. In the district that you represent, there are at least two factories that are facing a very serious and difficult situation due to importations in 1938 of shoes from the United States and under the new trade treaty the importations in this particular field will very definitely increase in 1939.
I myself last week saw samples of shoes that are to be purchased from the United States in quantities by one of our large retailing organizations and this business is coming directly out of factories in your own district. I urge you to give very serious consideration to this and I would appreciate an opportunity of personally discussing the shoe industry with you sometime when it is convenient to you.
Yours very truly,
Shoe Manufacturers' Association, W. H. Brimblecombe,
President.
To this the minister replied:
In reply to your letter of January 23 I wish to say that I have received no complaints from the local shoe manufacturers in Kitchener. I do not anticipate that the reductions which have been made in the new Canada-United States agreement will materially increase the importation of footwear.
I should point out that the tariff has been reduced on kid leather from 27J 'to 20 per cent. This is a valuable concession to the manufacturers of ladies' shoes. Excise tax will also be removed from a number of the materials used in the manufacture of footwear. I would be disappointed indeed if the shoe industry in this country is injured by the new agreement.
While I shall be glad to discuss matters with you at any time. I am bound to say that no change can be made in the agreement as it has already been signed.

Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
The last paragraph of that letter, Mr. Speaker, raises the whole question of the method followed by the government of this dominion in making trade agreements. We have heard considerable talk about the men who went over there and negotiated the details of the treaty. I knew Mr. McKinnon before he ever came down here, and I knew of Mr. Wilgress and Mr. Robertson, three capable men. I doubt if there is a man in any country anywhere who knows custom duties better than Mr. McKinnon; I have no hesitation in saying that. But Mr. McKinnon does not make trade treaties. All Mr. McKinnon does is to work out the intricate details of the treaty after the government has announced its policy. Mr. McKinnon worked out the increases in the tariff in 1930, and in the following year. He simply carries out whatever the tariff policy of the government is. And so, regardless of what is contained in this treaty, all that Mr. McKinnon and his assistants had to do with it was the working out of the various items and making one dovetail with the other. The policy itself is the policy of the government.
On the other hand, in the United States, they gave their people, regardless of what line of business they were engaged in, an opportunity to consider the trade treaty before it was concluded. The United States gave notice to all those likely to be affected in any way by the treaty, setting forth the various items that were to be considered. Every item that was to be considered when the United States negotiated its trade treaties with the United Kingdom and Canada was set forth in a pamphlet so that a man reading it could say: Well, this item does not affect me, so I do not have to bother. But if any item did affect him, he had the opportunity of going to Washington and laying his case before the men who were negotiating the treaty on behalf of the Washington government. That was also the procedure in England, and we can readily see that the men who went to Washington, representing the interests of United States industry, were certainly very successful in the pleas they made before the committee of inquiry.
But in Canada we knew nothing even as to the items that were to be considered, and we had no opportunity of going before any committee. The government may say: Well, you had a chance of coming down or sending in your brief. But since the items that were to be considered were not known, that would have meant that every industry in the country would have had to send in a brief to safeguard its interests-and judging by the treaty itself, certainly little consideration was given to the briefs that were placed before the government.
The shoe brief is a very fine example of how representations made to the government were ignored. Here was the policy of the government, a low tariff policy, and it was this policy of the government that the three men who negotiated on behalf of Canada at Washington were going to carry out. So I say, Mr. Speaker, that the whole basis on which we make trade agreements is wrong and unfair to this country, unfair to our vegetable and fruit growers, unfair to our farmers, unfair to the wheat growers of western Canada, unfair to industry generally.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Unfair to labour.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: They have no idea what labour is. One can easily understand a situation such as that when one realizes the set-up of the present cabinet. Perhaps one of the most remarkable things about our government is this. We have in it, I believe, eight lawyers, one newspaper publisher, one journalist, one university professor, three who are mentioned as farmers-one who was a school teacher who became a farmer; another used to be a farmer and since 1921 has been a very smart-I will not say statesman, shall I say politician?- and yet another who is no longer known as a farmer but is looked upon as a financier; I refer to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning).

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: He is the best of the lot.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
There are none more pleased than those engaged in industry that the Minister of Finance is back in his place in the house. I have no hesitation in saying that the one member of the government in whom the industrial workers and the heads of industry in this country feel they can have some confidence is the present Minister of Finance. But not one man belonging to that present cabinet has had any practical industrial experience. Not one man in that cabinet has had a close association with labour and knows what are the hours and conditions of labour. So one can easily understand why idealistic trade agreements are made with the United States and with Great Britain. It is not a policy of appeasement. The agreement was a business deal between Great Britain and the United States, with us in between, and as a result we are getting thoroughly squeezed.
I should have liked to deal at some length with the textile industry. I intend to go into that subject when the various items come up. But when we talk about the quotas which the United States give our primary producers in Canada, I should like to mention a few of
1398	COMMONS
Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
the quotas which are extended to other countries in which the standard of living is very low.
In 1937 Japan had 20 per cent of the cotton rayon bedspread business of Canada. In 1938 Japan had 72 per cent of that whole business, with the result that some of our industries could no longer produce any of these articles and had to close down. Of woollen textiles, 43 per cent of our total consumption was imported. As to worsted clothing, 65 per cent of the total consumed in Canada was imported.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Why?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Why? Because this government is more concerned about industrial workers in other countries than it is about our own. In Japan the wage rate in the textile industry is from 2 to 2} cents an hour. Japan must import its raw products from the southern states or from Egypt. The price of the raw products is just the same laid down in Japan as it is laid down in any city of Canada. But their workers are paid about 2| cents an hour. On the other hand there are codes in the Ontario law; we have to pay from 30 cents an hour upwards to our textile workers.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Did they pay that in 1935 and before that?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Do not answer relevant questions!

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
I may say this, that in all the time I have been engaged in industry' I have found that ninety-nine per cent of our industrial heads are fair to their employees if they are given a chance by the government in power. If they are unfair to their employees this government could take action against them and see to it that they are fair. Again I sayr that if this government had handled the whole situation as between themselves and the various provinces as they should have done, in a spirit of cooperation and with a determination to do something worth while for Canada and for the industrial workers, we should have had by this time unemployment insurance and decent labour laws throughout the dominion.
I have not time to take up another subject,-

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: The hon. member has done very well.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
-but I do say' this, that we are going to watch carefully' and with considerable interest how various hon. members on the Liberal side of the house vote with regard to this trade treaty. We shall see

whether they vote as their hearts dictate, or whether they vote as the Liberal whip dictates to them.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the remarks of the, hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth). He is a distinct asset to the Conservative party; his exposition of Conservative ideas upon this subject was an able one.
The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen), who preceded the hon. member for Waterloo South, said something about the Social Credit party7. Let me tell him that the Alberta government is generally recognized as the best government in Canada. It is cognizant of the situation as it exists. Perhaps the criticism by' the Right Hon. Oliver Stanley that some observations of his opponents were so much ey'ewash could be applied to certain hon. members who so inconsistently charge the Alberta government with inefficiency. That government has a policy of its own; it is developing in a new way the industries of the province. It is a characteristic of our party that it is always looking forward. On two occasions this afternoon we have heard questions about what happened in 1930 and even as far back as 1896. Apparently anything is good enough to conceal the urgencies of the present situation by references to what happened in the past. If anyone made an error in past years, it must be pointed to as something grievous and the party which made that error is deemed to be forever inimical to the welfare of the nation, although there is nothing we can do about it to-day.
I want hon. members to realize that our party is here as an independent group with our own ideas upon tariffs and economics generally'. The hon. member for Marquette flippantly mentioned this afternoon what he called economic nationalism. I wonder if he is able to define that term. I have seen many definitions of it. I have seen also many definitions of democracy. I know that communists call themselves the real democrats, that fascists style themselves socialistic or socialist democrats, and that all the parties in this house term themselves democrats. It is difficult indeed to understand the real meaning of words which are so glibly uttered by some hon. members in dealing with subjects upon which they seem to know hardly anything. Thus, at this moment, I had to rise to defend the government of Alberta, because that government has, in its own way and without recourse to tariffs, done something to develop the industry of the province.
We, as a group, are in favour of this trade treaty, and in my constituency most of the

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
people, I am sure, are in favour of it. That group of people whom I have the honour to represent are probably the most cosmopolitan in Canada. Besides the native-born Canadians we have people from all parts of Europe. While this treaty probably contains features that are not so acceptable to us, it is on the whole acceptable because it introduces a fresh spirit of understanding between the great English-speaking nations of the world. We must develop a spirit of friendship with Britain on the one hand, and with the United States on the other. To-day people travel more than they have ever done in the history of the world, and this year it is a good thing that the government have brought forward this treaty. It seems that various factors are working together at this time to promote the welfare of the Englishspeaking nations and to develop a spirit of harmony among these peoples. I do not know whether it was planned or not, but at any rate we have the great fair in New York which will bring many citizens from Europe, and in Canada we have the royal visit, which will also bring from Europe and the United States a great many visitors; and these visitors will all, to a certain degree, benefit through these trade agreements by purchases in Canada.
There is no doubt in my mind that trade agreements create harmony between peoples. In so far as this agreement affects western Canada, the two items that are of most interest to my district are those dealing with cattle and dairy products. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) this afternoon mentioned some modifications with respect to cattle. I did not get clearly what he said, but I shall be able to read it in Hansard to-morrow. As regards cattle I find this statement in the press release. On cattle weighing 700 pounds or more each there is a maximum reduction of 14 cents a pound, compared with two cents a pound under the 1935 trade agreement, and three cents a pound under the tariff act of 1930.
The new trade agreement provides that the maximum reduction in duty shall apply to
225,000	head imported in any one calendar year, of which not more than 60.000 head shall be imported during any one quarter of the calendar year. In other words, provision is made not only for a further reduction in duty by the maximum, but also for an increase in the annual quota to which the reduced duty applies of nearly 70.000 head over the quota provided for in the 1935 trade agreement. On calves the new trade agreement provides for the continuation of the reduced rate of 14 cents per pound accorded in the 1935 trade agreement as compared with the tariff rate of 24 cents per pound, but the tariff quota to which this reduced rate applies is increased from 51,933 head to 100,000 head in any one calendar year.
The weight bracket to which the reduced rate applies is also increased from 175 to 200 pounds, any calves weighing less than this being eligible for importation under the concession in the trade agreement. On dairy cows the concession in the 1935 trade agreement of the maximum reduction to 14 cents per pound is continued in the new trade agreement, but the quota limitation of 20,000 head in any one calendar year is abolished.
The new trade agreement provides for the maximum reduction in duty to 34 cents per gallon, the quantity of milk to be admitted at the reduced rate to be 3,000,000 gallons in any one calendar year.
And there is a further reduction of four cents a pound on cheese.
The hon. member for Waterloo South said that more milk and cream was produced in his constituency than required. At the same time, I would point out, we need some markets for our products abroad. At present vast quantities of butter have accumulated on the Canadian market, and something should be done to relieve this congestion of dairy products. Farmers generally are desirous that something should be done to-day to have more butter consumed in Canada, and if a certain quantity of milk is diverted to other markets it will, of course, relieve the situation in regard to butter and cheese.
An hon. member last w-eek said that we should play the game in this house, that nations should play the game with one another; and, of course, playing with other nations would cultivate a greater mutual respect. I admit that this is important, but we must exercise self-control in all things until it is reduced to a habit. We must take our losses as sportsmen, and if there are losses in the trade agreement, such as the six cents wheat preference in Britain, we should take them in a sporting spirit, realizing that the concessions cannot be all in our favour, that we must give some concessions in return. It is notable, in international trade, that nine-tenths of all our external trade was conducted last year with empire countries and with the United States. Much of the remainder was done with nations which are and always have been on friendly terms with this country. This, I think, proves that trade and goodwill among nations are reciprocal. No nation can live unto itself alone; we can induce other people to buy from us only by making it as easy as possible for them to sell to us.
During this debate we have heard much about the pride of the Liberal party in the achievements of Laurier and the pride of the Conservative party in those of Macdonald. A great deal has been said about the past. Well, we have threshed this old straw over and over again until we are sick and tired of
1400	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
hearing anything about it, and now we must look for the wheat. We have been told that it is only by working harder and harder, and so increasing the size of the cake, that we can hope for a larger slice. Now that a large cake has been produced, we are told that we cannot eat it because it is too large.
