maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with the utmost confidence in the beneficial results that are certain to accrue to the people of Canada from the new trade treaty with the United States that I rise to make a few observations. At the outset I wish most strongly to commend and to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and members of his government upon the splendid way in which they have, by various trade agreements, brought to still greater fruition the policy to which the Liberal party has pledged itself, year in and year out.
When in 1935 the Bennett-Manion government placed its future in the hands of the people, the cry of battle was met by the Liberal party with a well defined platform, calculated to assist the best interests of the dominion at large. And the electorate of Canada, having had full and plenty of Messrs. Bennett and Manion, returned Mr. Mackenzie
1402	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
King with the largest majority of supporters any party has ever had in the House of Commons.
The making of a trade treaty with the United States is no new policy of the Liberal party. Although defeated on a trade treaty in the general election of 1911, the Liberal party still continued to believe their trade policy was right. Back in 1923 the following resolution was debated in the House of Commons:
That the governor in council may authorize any minister of the crown to enter into negotiations with any authorized representative of the government of the United States with a view to the making of a commercial agreement between the two countries, on terms which may be deemed mutually beneficial. Any agreement so made shall be subject to the approval of the parliament of Canada.
In the debate which preceded the adoption of the resolution the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen declared the continuing opposition by the Conservative party to a policy of reciprocity. Mr. Fielding, supporting the resolution, made the following declaration:
Hon. gentlemen of the Conservative party, so far as they permit themselves to be represented by my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) are against any trade treaty with the United States. In the name of the Liberal party of Canada, I declare to-day that we stand for reciprocity with the United States. I say that when the opportunity comes to make a fair treaty or agreement, and the agreement of 1911 was a fair and reasonable agreement, we are proud to declare in the face of the parliament of Canada, whatever the fate o-f it may be, that this Liberal party stands for reciprocity with the United States when we can get a fair and reasonable agreement. That is our position. We are content to let the people judge between the honourable gentlemen and ourselves on that point.
Comparing the foregoing with the present attitude of the Liberal party, we readily see that the Liberal party has not deviated from its belief in the beneficial results to be had from reciprocity.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, from listening during the last few days to speeches made by hon. members opposite on the trade agreement, that their policy is no different from that of their predecessors, namely "no truck or trade with the Yankees." It would be interesting to know just how the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) feels about this agreement. I notice that at page 316 of Hansard for 1930, when he was Minister of Trade and Commerce in the Bennett government, and tariffs were being raised sky-high, he is reported to have said:
We are amending the tariff for the purpose of trying to reengage in the industries of Canada tens of thousands of honest Canadian citizens.

Again at page 318 he is reported as follows: -that the right hon. gentleman who is Prime Minister-
That is Mr. Bennett.
[DOT]-of this country to-day stands for a policy which has not had a trial in Canada for thirty-five years, a policy for the protection of Canadian industry. There has not been an opportunity up to the present time to give effect to that policy.
And again at page 319, he continued:
When these measures-
The new tariff.
-which are now in existence . . . are in full effect, they will provide work for some 30,000 to 50,000 industrialists in this country.
And at page 322 he continued:
Instead of quibbling about whether it is going to take the last of the 117,000 unemployed, we say that it will take the first 30,000 or
40,000	and therefore it is a worthy measure which should have the support of this house.
The same hon, member is reported to have written an open letter a few days later to his "fellow citizens." This letter, under date of October 4, 1930, is in part as follows:
Every year for the past few years, Canada has been importing $800,000,000 worth of merchandise that she might just as well have been producing from her own mines, or her own farms, or in her own factories. Some things, of course, like raw cotton and raw rubber, she must import. But making due allowance for such items the fact remains that $800,000,000 of her annual imports have been of a class or kind that she was quite capable of producing for herself. With the aid of statistics giving the annual value of Canadian factory production, and the number of persons employed therein, it requires little figuring to-show that every $5,600 worth of goods turned out has meant a job for one person. Assuming that something close to that ratio would hold good as the average for all classes of products, it follows that were we to produce in Canada the $800,000,000 worth of merchandise that we have been importing unnecessarily, we would be giving employment to 147,527 workers more than are now employed, to say nothing of the thousands of others to whom employment would come indirectly, as a result of this new stimulus to business in general. Now do you see how true it is that were we all to practise a little intelligent discrimination in our daily buying, our unemployment problem would quickly and permanently disappear ?
It will be seen from this letter that the hon. member attempted to explain in detail why and how the Canada-first tariff, enacted in September, 1930, would bring Canada's unemployed back to work. But I submit that time has proven that this policy of economic nationalism did not lessen unemployment, but on the contrary increased it. All of which proves that high tariffs increase unemployment. Apparently by 1932 the hon. gentleman

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
had a change of heart in regard to the matter of national policy, as is indicated by his remarks on the Canada-United States trade agreement of 1935. Supporting the trade agreement resolution before the house he made the following statement, to be found on page 723 of Hansard for 1936:
About 1932, in view of conditions that were developing the world over and the inhibitions against Canadian exports entering other countries, I felt that quotas, import restrictions, the raising of tariffs, what is commonly called a national spirit, which was so prevalent and is still so prevalent throughout the world, placed many obstacles in the way of our trade and in the way of trade generally. I felt it was highly desirable that Canada should study the trade relations between our country and the United States, and with that in mind I instructed the staff under me at the time to proceed to a study of the trade between the two countries, and to prepare in detail the items upon which without injury to ourselves and in all fairness to the United States we might offer some considerations for favourable trade.
The above is indeed a far cry from the economic nationalism which he had championed so ardently a few years previously. It is apparent that his leader, if consistent, will vote against the resolution, because referring to the possible results of the treaty, he said, as reported on page 1066 of Hansard of this year:	,
Time alone will tell, but my belief is that the ill effects will be very much greater than the good effects.
Certainly no one would vote against his own better judgment. The question in many minds is: What will be the position taken by our chameleon friend, the hon. member for Kootenay East.
I should like to deal for a moment with some of the remarks made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), which were referred to later by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion). At page 912 of Hansard the hon. leader of the opposition is reported as follows:
I do not want to puncture the bubble the right hon. gentleman has been blowing, but at the same time I do not think it is necessary to get quite so much excited about the marvellous peace treaty which has been negotiated by the right hon. gentleman to keep the United States and Canada and the United States and Great Britain from going to war.
And again at page 1050 of Hansard the leader of the opposition is reported as saying:
The right hon. gentleman talked as if this was not a trade treaty but a peace treaty. As I listened to him, I thought he spoke, as if we had just been engaged in a spectacular war with some great nation and had won a glorious victory;
And again:
He spoke as if we had won some great victory, and yet, as I pointed out the other night, not. since 1812, a period of over a hundred years, have we had any differences of a serious nature with the United States, and certainly since the beginning of the century there have been no differences between Great Britain and the United States.
What the right hon. Prime Minister did say and to which the hon. leader of the opposition took exception is to be found on
page 910 of Hansard:
Once again we have played the part of reconciling and interpreting the two great Englishspeaking nations to each other. The making of these agreements, especially when the world situation is so precarious as it unfortunately is, is an achievement of superlative importance, which will have its repercussions throughout the world in the next generation. In the present, each of us sleeps more safely in his bed because of the rapproachement between the world's two greatest democracies, a rapproachement that could not have been effected without the assent and the cooperation of Canada. If this administration were to end to-morrow, it would have its honourable place in world history on this score alone. That is the broad fact of the present situation. Like Canning, we have done our indispensable part to call into existence a "new world to redress the balance of the old."
And again at page 911:
The trade agreements concluded between Canada and the United States, and Great Britain and the United States constitute the one outstanding contribution of our times toward economic disarmament. As such, they have immeasurably helped to create a basic situation more favourable to peaceful relations between nations ... It is deeply gratifying to the government that ... we w-ere able to further not only the ends of commerce and trade but the all important ends of international goodwill.
At the imperial conference of 1937, the representatives of the several governments concerned had under review the possibility of reviving confidence and increasing the stability of economic and financial conditions in the world, a process which they considered essential to the prosperity of individual countries as well as to international peace. In order to assist in furthering this end, they declared themselves ready to cooperate with other nations in examining current difficulties, including trade barriers and other obstacles to the increase of international trade and the improvement of the general standard of living. The imperial conference also declared :
The outstanding feature of the discussion was the emphatic desire expressed by the representatives of every part of the British commonwealth represented at the conference, that all practicable steps should be taken to secure the stimulation of international trade. It was recognized that in the last resort, the prosperity
1404	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
of the countries of the commonwealth depends on that of the world as a whole, and that a healthy growth of international trade, accompanied by an improvement in the general standard of living, is an essential step to political appeasement.
Surely the above declaration will convince even the most doubtful that there is a close connection between international trade and international peace. The trend of the speeches of the opposition has been to create a feeling of gloom as to Canada's future. Might I suggest at this point that it would be well for them to try to inspire the people with a spirit of confidence in their country. The Hon. Colonel J. L. Ralston some time ago, in an address to the presidents of the life insurance companies of America, stated, "Confidence feeds on confidence." Might it not be to the better advantage of Canada for these gloom-mongers to change their line of talk in keeping with the above, and thus do their part to promote confidence in Canada's economic future?
I should like to turn now to a consideration of what this treaty will mean to our people. Members from other sections of the country have already indicated the benefits that will accrue to the people in their respective districts. My remarks will be more or less confined to the benefits that the maritime provinces will derive from this agreement. I shall deal first with our export trade, consisting in great part of fish, lumber, potatoes, apples and foxes. I shall not take up the time of the house in discussing the latter four items because the hon. Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley), in his speech the other afternoon, dealt very effectively with the apple industry, and other hon. members from the maritimes have shown the likely improvements in the lumber, potato and fox industries.
But I might say in passing that at the annual meeting of the councillors of the municipality of Antigonish, a resolution was passed offering free to young men, farms which belonged to the municipality, the only condition being that these young men should operate the farms and pay the taxes for five years, after which time they would be given the deeds of the property. I learn from the municipal clerk that this offer has attracted many applicants from various parts of the province who are anxious to start out for themselves in the farming industry. I suggest that the government should make it as easy as possible for these young farmers to get government loans to help them stock and equip these farms, thus putting themselves in a position to take advantage of the benefits of the trade treaty.

I am lately in receipt of a copy of a resolution of protest passed by the Antigonish county farmers' association based on an intimation they received of a sales tax about to be imposed by the government on certain materials used in making balanced rations for poultry and live stock. But on inquiry I was glad to learn from the Minister of National Revenue that such is not the case, that there has never been any intention on the part of the government to impose such a tax. At this point, I should like to say that I was pleased to note that the government was able to reduce the duty on corn, a reduction which will represent an immense saving to our farmers.
Referring to the fishing industry, with the kind permission of the house I wish to put on Hansard a statement indicating the benefits which the fishermen of the maritimes will derive from the new trade agreement, based on the quantities of fish shipped to the United States in 1936 and 1937. This statement includes only fish known to have been produced and shipped from Atlantic coast waters, and does not take into consideration salmon, halibut and tuna, which would considerably increase the given figures, but for these items figures separate from Pacific coast shipments were not available. My object in preparing this statement is to show in definite figures the extra amounts which the fishermen would have enjoyed in those years had the present treaty duties been in effect. In 1936 this amount was $221,738.61, and in 1937, $184,076.46, money which would have represented a great boon to maritime fishermen. Estimating that the shipments of these classes of fish for the present year will even approximate those of either 1936 or 1937, we can easily see what a benefit the fishermen will derive, and I think it is quite safe to say that with this added impetus the fish export business will increase materially over the figures for either of the given years.
But our maritime fishermen, whose gear has been seriously destroyed in the recent storms, will need some real government assistance to repair and replace their losses, and thus enable them to carry on the fishing business in a worth while way, so that they will be in a position to avail themselves of the benefits indicated in the treaty.
The benefits which the consumer will receive from this trade agreement must not be overlooked. Many articles of every-day use, such as foodstuffs, clothing, et cetera, will be reduced in price, thereby tending to lower the cost of living. The producer also will benefit from the lower prices he will have to pay for articles of production-fishermen's

Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
supplies, dairy and horticultural machinery, fertilizers, et cetera. Personally, Mr. Speaker, I think this government deserves great credit for being able to consummate an agreement such as this presently being discussed without having made any concessions on coal, which means a great deal not only to the miners in the maritimes, but to those interested in many other branches of industry, such as the farmer, fisherman, lumberman, manufacturer, railroad man and others.
To put our people of the maritimes in a position to take advantage of the benefits of this trade agreement there are suggestions I should like to make to the government. I believe there should be a revision of the freight rates. From a recent issue of the Halifax Chronicle I learn that Mr. Rand H. Matheson, manager of the maritime transportation commission, told an Amherst audience that a revision of our freight rates is essential to meet changing conditions in transportation, as well as to establish a complete parity with rates granted certain types of freight in upper Canada.
While on the subject of transportation, I wish to draw to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) and the other members of the government, a most unfortunate situation existing in my constituency. In Guysborough county there are thousands of acres of standing timber that cannot be cut and put on the market for the very simple reason that we have no means of transporting it.

As many hon. members probably know, there is a limited distance in which lumber can be hauled profitably with teams, also a limited distance in which it can be hauled by auto truck, which means that there remain only two profitable methods of transportation, namely, rail and water. In this instance the haul to the waterfront is too long, and we have no railroad. The construction of what was known as the Guysborough railway was started in 1929 by the then government, under the leadership of the present Prime Minister. But after several millions had already been spent on the construction of the railway, and although there was a great number of unemployed in the country at the time, the government which succeeded
my right hon. leader's government in 1930 issued instructions that the work on the railway should be stopped. To those, of course, who know the political record of the constituency, the reason for such an order is quite obvious. I hope, however, it is not the intention of this present government, again under the leadership of my right hon. leader, to allow the money that has already been spent on this project to be entirely lost. In this connection may I quote from an editorial which appeared some months ago in The Eastern Chronicle, a newspaper published in Nova Scotia, headed "Guysborough railway" :
No sadder picture can be imagined than to drive through that country and note the political ruins of that enterprise. The grading has been completed and is now growing grass. The right-of-way belongs to the government, having been purchased and paid for. The concrete abutments for bridges are in place. All seems ready for the ties, rails, steel bridges and the station houses and platforms. As it stands to-day, it is a travesty upon the viciousness of party politics. For half a century the road has figured in public debates and in 1910 a contract was let and a change of government cancelled it.

speechtext:
I continue with the quotation from The Eastern Chronicle:
In 1926 negotiations for its construction were again resumed and a contract let to the Dominion Construction Company. Actual work was undertaken and the present state of the road reached, when a change of government took place in 1930, when there developed the most callous instance of political rancour ever displayed. The work was immediately abandoned. The steel for rails and bridges assembled on cars at Stellarton -were distributed elsewhere and people of that long-suffering county made to suffer for their political sins. It was rabid Toryism run wild.
The need for this railway was just as evident in 1930 as it was in 1926. The need is just as evident to-day. If the Liberal government of 1926 was justified in starting the work, as it was, that same justification exists to-day.
Might we point out several pertinent things with respect to the Guysborough railway. It is intended to tap a county that has no other
1406	COMMONS
Canada-United. States Trade Agreement
railway connection. It is the great unspoiled and undeveloped county of the maritimes. Guysborough county possesses a potential fishery wealth such as no other stretch of coast line in Canada, but alas, those sturdy fishermen of that coastal county have no means of transportation by which to market the product of the sea that comes in such great quantities to its shore.
Again Guysborough county has a great lumber wealth. This is evident by the use made in that regard of the first ten miles from Sunny Brae, where the projected road contacted the established railway. On this ten miles, rails were laid during construction and have been maintained in semi-fashion since for the movement of lumber freight. This information is furnished by one who should know, and is to the effect that upon that short section of rough road there originated more freight than on any like branch in the Canadian National railway system.
Another important item at this juncture in unemployment would be the completion of the railway. The rails and bridges would give direct employment to the steel workers-both manufacturing and fabricating. The ties and the station houses would employ lumber from our own woods. In fact, the completion of the road w'ould call for, first, the utilization of our natural products; and, second, the employment of local labour.
The prospects of this road are not to be overlooked. Tapping as it will the great fishery resources, should bring to its support the Minister of Fisheries. The agricultural possibilities are in keeping with that reached by any maritime road. The magnificent St. Mary's valleys are an instance. Although now miles away from the rails they are productive and prosperous, and, had they transport connection, their wealth could be enormously increased. The region through which the railway projects is a sportsman's paradise and can be developed into a holiday seeker's mecca.
These arguments are old and oft repeated, but the repetition has not detracted from their truth, as a true story cannot die of old age.
But over all is the necessity of keeping faith *with the people of Guysborough county. They have been falsely and traitorously dealt with. They have been made a cat's paw of a Tory majority in Ontario or some other section, and such wretched intolerance should not be permitted to obtain.
I want to tell members of this house, and especially the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), the Minister of Transport, and their colleagues, that this section of Canada needs a railway to open up and develop this territory which can be developed in no other way. Lumber, farming, fishing and mining would all benefit, and the development of these industries naturally would mean employment- a livelihood for many of our people, which in turn would mean greater liquid wealth which would undoubtedly help the railroads, steamship companies, manufacturers and many others. I cannot urge too strongly on the members of this government the great possibilities that exist for the development of

the natural resources of Guysborough, if this railway is completed. The hardwood areas alone are something that, within ten years, are going to be of inestimable value. I might remind the ministers that there is still considerable unemployment in our country, although we do not hear so much about it as in some sections, because our people are the type who tighten up their belts, so to speak, and endure with patience all manner of hardships and suffering before resorting to relief.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
They have to, under this
government.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
And they had to do plenty of it between 1930 and 1935. This unemployment situation is just one more reason why I implore this government to complete the construction of the Guysborough railroad as soon as possible.
Before concluding my remarks, I wish to refer to the Saint Francis Xavier university extension movement which has for some years been cooperating with the various departments of government. Their activities are many and varied, and there is no doubt that they are assisting our primary producers in a way that will help them to profit to an even greater extent from the trade treaty.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I cannot agree with the remarks of my friend the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Fleming), who thinks that the government should not go to the country this year. On the contrary, my opinion is that the record of the Mackenzie King government is such that they can go to the country at any time and receive a mandate from the people to continue to carry on their good work.
Mr. ROWE (Dufferin-Simeoe); They will get the same result, no matter when they go.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to-day I propose to discuss this Canada-United States trade agreement, and the concessions which have been made by Canada under the United Kingdom-Canada agreement, from the point of view of those Canadians who live on the Pacific slope, the people of British Columbia-that great province which is rapidly becoming the third province in Canada in population, but is furthest from the centre of Canada, and with problems so different from the rest of Canada -problems which we feel are often so little understood by the other Canadians. Incidentally, no individuals could do more than members of this house to help in the understanding of our problems. They are all in a

Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
position of influence, and they all have free transportation, both for themselves and for their families. I suggest to them that during the coming summer those who have not been to the Pacific coast should visit our province. Hon. members on the other side may not have an opportunity to do so under the same favourable conditions next year. We shall be very glad to have them with us before the unhappy event. That invitation is extended particularly to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and to the senior members of his cabinet, who have been conspicuous by their absence from British Columbia since the election campaign of four years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: We have been too busy here.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
To understand the effect of this agreement and of these concessions on British Columbia, one must bear in mind two facts, which I should like to stress. First, British Columbia is primarily a lumber province, with the bulk of the lumbering done in the coast region, where we have the famous Douglas fir. The second fact which should be borne in mind is that the neighbouring states of Washington and Oregon are also on the Pacific slope, and that they occupy much the same position in the United States as British Columbia occupies in Canada, producing much the same products and giving us the stillest kind of competition, for example, in lumbering, fruit growing and fishing. These two states have a much larger population than British Columbia, and their people have much more capital behind them than our people. Also they have in the other states of the union a much larger home market than British Columbia has in the other provinces of this dominion.
It so happens that lumbering and fruit growing are the two industries in our province which are most affected by this United States agreement and by the concessions Canada has made under the United Kingdom agreement. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) has dealt with the fruit growing industry, and I do not intend to deal with it to-day, but I do propose to deal with the industry of lumbering, which is our greatest and most important industry.
I am glad to be able to do so, because the government can do something further for the lumber industry, whereas it cannot do anything for any other industry. A discussion on lumbering is not purely academic, as it is with respect to other Canadian industries. I say this because under the Canada-United States agreement lumber, and lumber alone, is dealt with in two stages, the first stage 71492-89
coming into force with the rest of the treaty on January 1 of this year, the second stage coming into force only if, as and when the United States sees fit to remove its import excise tax of $1.50 per thousand feet board measure. In other words, the bargain on lumber is not yet concluded, although this government have put Canada in the weak position of binding herself in advance to make further great concessions in lumber if the United States chooses to bring in the second stage by dropping its import excise tax.
Incidentally, the United States is not bound to drop that excise tax; it is not bound to bring in the second stage of the lumber bargain. But I do suggest that the government's job on lumber is only half done, and I urge upon them at once to bring all possible pressure to bear on the United States not to renew this import excise tax when it expires at the end of June of this year. I urge that because the first stage of the lumber bargain is all one-sided, and unless this second stage is brought into force the agreement will have been most unfair to the lumber industry; certainly there will have been a great injustice done to the thousands of people engaged in that industry in British Columbia, to thousands of others engaged in dependent industries, and, in fact, to people in almost every walk of life in our province.
That brings me to a consideration of just what this stage of the lumber bargain is. But as a background, and so that the real effects of this Canada-United States agreement and the concessions Canada has made under the Canada-United Kingdom agreement may be clearly seen, I should like to sketch roughly the history of the lumbering industry in the coast area of British Columbia during the last decade. I deal with that area alone because while there is lumbering done in other parts of the province, the industry is largely centred in the wet belt which is known as the coast area.
The story of lumber in that area for the past ten years is quite a romantic tale. In 1929, just ten years ago, that area sold approximately 1,040,000,000 feet board measure of lumber in Canada, in our home market, the best market any industry can have. We sold a little more than half that amount, namely 540,000,000 board feet, in the United States. In the United States market we had free entry-no duty, no excise tax. We had had free entry since 1913. We sold only 70,000,000 feet to the United Kingdom where at that time, of course, we had no preference, and we sold, including the 70,000,000 feet to Great Britain, a total of 160,000,000 feet tc

1408	COMMONS
Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
the empire. In addition, we sold 240,000,000 feet to foreign lands, principally Japan and China.
I propose to say nothing further about the home market, except that it fell with the depression and has risen again until in 1937 it was about 565,000,000 feet; or about the foreign market, except that it has gone on much the same as in 1929, now up, now down; at the present time it is below 100,000,000 feet, largely because of the trouble in Asia.
I deal particularly with our markets in the United States, the United Kingdom and the British empire. In 1930 the United States passed the Hawley-Smoot tariff, the highest, I believe, in the modern history of the United States. That tariff imposed a duty of $1 per thousand feet against Canadian lumber, with the result that in 1931 our sales to the United States had dropped by about one-half, while our sales to the empire remained about the same. Not content with the Hawley-Smoot tariff the United States in 1932 passed a Revenue Act, which imposed an import excise tax of $3 per thousand feet, making a hurdle of $4 per thousand feet to be overcome by our lumber going into the United States. That hurdle was prohibitive.
Hon. members should bear in mind at all times that this business of raising high levies, this business of stopping trade, was started not by Canada but by the United States. Our lumber market was placed in such a position by this hurdle of $4 per thousand feet that a substitute market simply had to be found, and fortunately the Bennett government were able to negotiate in 1932 the empire agreements which gave us, generally speaking, a preference of ten per cent. As a result of these two moves-the United States raising its levies and Great Britain and other parts of the empire giving us a preference- in 1933 British Columbia sold in the United States only 30,000,000 feet as against over 540,000,000 feet in 1929; but despite the depression, our sales to Great Britain went up from 70,000,000 feet in 1929 to 270,000,000 feet in 1933, having increased about four times, and our sales to the empire rose from 160,000,000 feet in 1929 to 430,000,000 feet in 1933. By 1935 our sales to the United States were up to 95,000,000 feet, still very low, while our sales to the United Kingdom were 455,000,000 feet, and to the empire, 635,000,000 feet. The empire trade was steadily increasing.
In the fall of 1935 this government came into office and negotiated the Canada-United States agreement, which cut in half the duty and import excise tax, totalling S4 per thou-

sand feet, subject to a quota of 250,000,000 feet in any one year for Douglas fir and western hemlock, which are the two types of lumber we produce in the largest quantities. That first Canada-United States agreement has been a great disappointment to the lumber industry of British Columbia. In the years following the negotiation of the treaty Canada has never been able to sell the quota. The nearest approach was in 1938 when we sold approximately 170,000,000 feet, or about seventy per cent. But on the other side of the picture our sales to the United Kingdom have climbed and climbed until in 1938 we sold to Great Britain 740,000,000 feet- more lumber than we have ever sold to the United States in one year. To the empire as a whole we sold last year 960,000,000 feet, quite an increase from 160,000,000 feet in 1929-all as a direct result of the preference given us by the empire trade agreements.
Now this present government boast of increasing export trade. They boast of the great treaties they have negotiated, but they never have achieved anything like the empire agreements, and I do not believe they ever will. If they ever did achieve agreements of that type, we would be kept here for five years hearing all the talk about the wonderful things that had been done.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: May I ask a question?

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Ask it after dinner. The United States sums up the situation very clearly in its press release dealing with the United Kingdom agreement. At page 36 we find:
The position with regard to a number of important individual products is even more unsatisfactory than that with regard to the wood group as a whole, since there has been, as a result of the import duties, a very serious diversion of the trade from the United States to empire countries in several products, notably Douglas fir and certain other softwood lumber, plywood, and doors. In the case of doors, the United Kingdom had taken-
"Had" taken, mark you.
-as high as 94 per cent of the United States total annual exports, but the increase in 1935 in the duty to 2s. 6d. per door has almost eliminated American competition. One of the major objectives of the present trade agreement has been, therefore-
This is the United States speaking.
-to restore as far as possible the competitive position of the United States as a supplier of these products which have been so seriously affected by empire preference in the United Kingdom.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: I know that very well ; I was there when it was amended, and I will express my view about the amendment, which makes the bill more unsound legally.

Might we have the

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext:
The following' is to be added to subsection 2:
Subject to all provincial and municipal enactments in respect to highways and motor vehicles operated thereon, and applicable thereto.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: Thank you, sir. The story behind this bill is that in the year of grace 1925 the city of Quebec entered into a contract with the Quebec Light, Heat and Power Company, or the Quebec Railway Company, by virtue of which an exclusive thirty year franchise was granted by the city for trolley car operation.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: What was the date of the contract?

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext:
It was granted in 1925, so
the thirty year franchise would extend to the year of grace 1955.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: That was between the city of Quebec and the company?

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext:
Yes. Last fall another agreement was entered into in order that the same exclusive franchise might include the operation of buses until the year of grace 1955. The bill is interesting, but the bad part of it is still more interesting. I am strongly opposed to any exclusive franchise. I am for competition. I know it is pretty hard to have street railway competition in a city like Quebec because it might turn out as badly as it did in Detroit; they might become bankrupt. A certain privilege is required for 71492-89J
the construction of railway lines on the streets of a city, but when it comes to the operation of a bus service the situation is entirely different. In the first place, I do not see why this company should have an exclusive franchise for the operation of buses within the city of Quebec. I would ask hon. members to read the explanatory note, which contains the words "in and in the neighbourhood of the city of Quebec." What is the neighbourhood of the city of Quebec? Does it extend to Riviere du Loup, which is 120 miles away?

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: Just a moment; my hon. friend may answer my questions in due course. I want to know; I do not want "no." It may come as far west of Quebec as the beautiful Gatineau hills. Then these people of the Quebec Railway Company will take advantage of this legislation to say, "we have an enactment of the dominion parliament granting us a franchise. Therefore all you other owners of buses get down into the ditch when we pass along. We are masters of the highway." I am not for this legislation, I am all against it.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend
for saying "hear, hear." There are some members of this committee who are opposed to all exclusive franchises, some of whom spoke on behalf of this bill in committee the other day. But I will not insist on that any longer. My first point is that the granting of any exclusive privileges is against all principles of Liberalism, and I am strongly opposed to it.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: Is that not a strange reason, coming from that side of the house?

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext:
Well, if my eyes do not deceive me, this bill comes from that side of the house. But I hope to make conversions by explaining my point of view. There is something else. If there is an exclusive franchise there must be some control of rates. Will that control be exercised by the public utilities commission of the province of Quebec or by the transport board that we have here in Ottawa? We are facing a dilemma. We are told that the company has a federal charter, which it obtained some forty years ago in order to secure a federal subsidy. Since then, however, most of their legislation has been provincial; many times the city of Quebec has made agreements with

Quebec Railway, Light and Power
this company, which agreements have been sanctioned by provincial legislation. That is known to everyone who is fond of reading provincial statutes. Who will exercise control in connection with rates? Will it be the public utilities commission of Quebec or will it be the federal transport board? It will be neither. This legislation is hybrid; it is illegitimate. If we had no lady members of this house I would use other and possibly stronger expressions.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: I am not asking what those expressions may be, but I really should like to understand why this company will not come under either provincial or federal control with regard to rates.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: My hon. friend, who has been a professor of philosophy, knows very well that the first part of a discussion is the status quaestionis, the statement of the question, and afterwards we make due distinctions. I hope my hon. friend will not ask me to define the Quebec utilities commission or the federal transport board, which he understands very well, I am sure, as all members of the committee do.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: If I understood the hon. member aright, he said the control over rates would not come under either body, and I do not understand that statement.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for his question, and I hope that by explaining the matter clearly I may bring him to agree with me. The chairman of the transport board has expressed himself clearly in regard to the operation of buses; this matter does not come under the transport board except perhaps-he was not sure of that- in the case of bus companies operating between two provinces or between one province and a foreign country such as the United States. His doubt was on this ground, that at first the railway commision was appointed to study and decide upon railway lines and railway questions. Later, its powers were extended, but not to include bus companies operating only within a province. That is the point. And by stating in the explanatory note to the bill that the bus company is operating within the limits and in the neighbourhood of the city of Quebec, we are to presume that the operations will not be outside the province of Quebec.
Moreover, the company cannot come under the jurisdiction of the transport board, unless it is stated that the buses will operate between two provinces, or between one province and a foreign country. That is an important point. Therefore it is beyond doubt
(Mr. Pouliot.]
that the transport board has no authority whatever over the rates on the buses which will be operated by the company within the city of Quebec or in the neighbourhood of that city, whatever that neighbourhood may include. If I have not made myself clear on this point, I would suggest that hon. members ask me to be more precise. That, however, is the first point.
Then there was an amendment which made the bill still worse. Our contention was that this parliament has no authority whatever upon the operation of buses, because they come under provincial jurisdiction entirely. The provinces impose licences on buses, and we have no authority whatever, because they use the kings highway for their operations and, according to the law and according to the general understanding, we have nothing whatever to do with buses.
Although I am not sure, because I had occasion to leave the committee for a few moments, I believe an amendment was suggested by the legal representative of the Department of Transport. He suggested an addition to the bill whereby it should be subject to all provincial and municipal regulations. As hon. members know very well, this parliament has no authority whatever with regard to municipal matters. All those things come under the exclusive jurisdiction of provincial legislatures; everyone knows that. Therefore, if there is an appendix to the bill to the effect that the whole matter will be subject to provincial and municipal regulations, there is the implication that it cannot be subject to the regulations of the transport board. It would come only under provincial jurisdiction, and therefore we would have no jurisdiction at all to include buses in the powers granted to the company.
If hon. members were to take the trouble to read section 8 of chapter 59 of the statutes of 1895, they would find the following in the explanatory note:
The company may use and employ for locomotion and propulsion of its cars, vehicles and rolling stock, where such power is required, electricity in all its forms, steam and any approved mechanical power or other means, agency or force for such purpose that science or invention may develop, and shall have all rights, powers, privileges-
And so on. We will notice the expression "electricity in all its forms, steam and any approved mechanical power or other means, agency or force for such purpose that science or invention may develop." They already have the power to operate any kind of vehicles, including buses or steam engines. But they come here to ask us for some privileged federal legislation, and I am opposed to it.

Quebec Railway, Light and Power
They say a serious doubt was expressed by all concerned-referring to the authority of the board of transport-which I denied, of course. No learned counsel appearing for the company or for the city of Quebec dared to affirm or to state that the board of transport had any authority to fix rates.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: What would my hon. friend offer in place of this bill? What would he substitute?

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext:
I would substitute nothing, because I assume I would suggest the withdrawal of the bill. This is none of our business. We are here asked to ratify a private agreement between a railway company and the city of Quebec; that is what is behind the bill. Before that, when the same thing occurred, the company and the city of Quebec went to the legislature to have their agreements confirmed. Now for the first time they come before the federal parliament and ask us to do what was done before by the Quebec legislature, namely to confirm a private agreement. We have nothing whatever to do with it.
If the travelling public go to the board of transport they will be told by the chairman and the learned commissioners that they have nothing to do with it, because they have no control whatever over bus services, and that it is a provincial matter. If the company is brought before the public utilities commission of the province of Quebec, it will argue that that body has no authority. The company will say, "our power to operate buses has been granted to us by the dominion parliament; therefore we deny the jurisdiction of the Quebec utilities commission." Then the people of the province of Quebec will complain about the high rates imposed upon them by the company, with the assent of the city of Quebec-which does not make it any better. The people will have to incur heavy expenditures to have writs of certiorari, and so on, to bring the matter before another court, if they can. They will be in a muddle of procedure-and in the meantime they will be paying high rates to travel on those buses. That is one point.
Every member of the committee knows very well that the private legislation passed by any provincial legislature, and by the dominion parliament as well, is a shameful queue to the statute books of the country. There are very few pieces of private legislation which can stand. Nearly every piece of private legislation is pure rot, and this time the Quebec Railway Company comes, with the assent of the city of Quebec, to secure from this
dominion parliament an exclusive franchise- under disguise. And in virtue of that amphibious legislation, when the people of the city of Quebec and the surrounding neighbourhood -which might be the whole province, because no one knows the ambitions of the president of the Quebec Railway Company, and his associates-

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: Who is the president?

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: I assume it is Julian C. Smith. When those people desire to extend the operation of the bus company to all boundaries of the province of Quebec, and whenever a man, or two men, or ten men, or scores, or hundreds of men complain of the high rates imposed upon them by the company, they will go to the board of transport, where they will be told that there is no jurisdiction and that they should go to the Quebec utilities commission. If they follow that advice, they will apply to the Quebec utilities commission, but they will be told by that commission that they have no jurisdiction. That commission will contend that, as the company is operating under a federal bill giving it the power to operate buses, they can do nothing and the people must suffer an injustice. The people will then curse the dominion parliament and will write to the hon. members who voted for this bill. They will be told they were wrong in thinking the bill was innocuous, that it covered simply an agreement between the city and the railway company.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: Would not the amendment submitted by the Department of Transport and accepted by the committee protect the government and the city of Quebec? I did not understand it thoroughly, but that amendment was accepted unanimously in the committee.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: I am just coming to that point. A learned counsel of the department, who is just as familiar with the law as I am with astronomy-it is a very dark night to-night-approved that amendment. What power do we have to state in our legislation that it shall be subject to provincial or municipal regulation?

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: The amendment protects the provincial rights.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext:
No. My hon. friend is good enough to listen to my argument, and I want to try to satisfy his mind entirely. This parliament has exclusive jurisdiction in certain matters, and the provincial legislatures have exclusive jurisdiction in other matters. I

Quebec Railway, Light and Power
think my hon. friend will agree with me on that. If we have jurisdiction to pass legislation giving the railway company the right to operate buses, then we also have the right to regulate the rates to be charged on those buses.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext:
If it does not interfere
with provincial rights.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: No. I want my hon. friend to listen to me. I have not finished, but I am on the eve of finishing my remarks. If we have jurisdiction to grant to the railway company the right to operate buses, then we also have the right to regulate the rates charged for travel on those buses. That is clear and evident. If, for the sake of appearance, we add the words "subject to provincial and municipal regulation," that means that the provincial and municipal regulations are intra vires of the province and the municipality and we have no right whatever.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: I do not think the committee had any jurisdiction to decide what are provincial and federal rights. They were just considering a bill, and an amendment was accepted to provide that we should not interfere with provincial rights.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: I was there when the vote was called, and I said "on division." I did not want to hold the bill in committee; I wanted it to come to the house. I am explaining this as clearly as I can. If the provinces have power to make regulations as to rates, then we have none. If we have the power, they have none.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: That is not for the committee to decide.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext:
The committee of the
whole can decide whatever it wants to. I am here to express my views, and I shall express them. It takes some time to understand a legal question of this kind, but the more complicated it is, the more interesting it is. Why have we to rely upon provincial authority for regulations in this matter? If we have no authority, what is the use of passing vague legislation like this to deceive the people and to embarrass all concerned? The people in Quebec are bound to use these buses because there is no competition. There is bound to be plenty of trouble because the company will rely upon the fact that there is no jurisdiction in the board of transport or the Quebec utilities commission to deal with complaints about rates. I would thank the sponsor of this bill to give us a little more explanation about the matter.
[Mt. Pouliot.]

speakeroldname: Mr. CHARLES PARENT (Quebec West and South):
subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). First of all, let me assure him that it is not our intention to operate autobuses in his constituency. All we are asking by this bill is the right to clarify a certain clause in the original charter granted in 1895. At that time there were no buses and no one had foreseen this new method of transportation. We claim that the original charter covers whatever forms of transportation science may discover. There has been a demand in the city of Quebec for an improvement in the transportation system. The same is true of many other cities. The people are asking for motor-buses.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext: Would the hon. member mind speaking a little louder? I think the Hansard reporter is having difficulty in hearing his remarks.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext:
That shows the necessity for some amplifying system in the chamber.
There are in the city of Quebec at the present time some autobuses which have been used there for a few months, running out to a little suburb about three miles outside the city. That territory was actually covered by the Quebec railway with a tramway line, but under the pressure of the population of Sillery the tramway service was replaced by autobuses. The company is bringing this bill forward under pressure of public demand. In my own county of Quebec West and South we have a tramway' line which was laid thirty-five years ago and is still in operation, but some people have to walk ten or fifteen blocks before they can get the tram.
It is easy, when a company comes to parliament asking for certain powers, for someone to raise the cry of trusts and make all kinds of charges, but anyone who is familiar with local conditions would not be opposed to this bill. It has been submitted to the civic authorities in the city of Quebec, and I do not see why there should be so much blowing of bubbles over such an insignificant amendment, because we have all the protection that is afforded by our committee on railways and canals. There is nothing in this bill to confer an exclusive franchise or to interfere with the rights of anyone else who wants to start some other transportation system or autobuses.
The Quebec Railway is a company that has invested about $20,000,000 in the tramway system in the city of Quebec, and autobuses are being asked for practically unanimously

Quebec Railway, Light and Power
by the people of that city. Anyone who knows how narrow the streets are in the city of Quebec, and how the tramway line obstructs traffic, will be in favour of this bill. It is all very well for the hon. member to rise in his place and say that Julian C. Smith is president of the company. Yes, he is the president of the company because he has proved that he knows something about transportation and the electrical systems of this country. He knows that what he is asking for here is tc meet a public demand, ai 1 the company would not be seeking to spend money od autobuses if it were not that there is a public demand for them. After all, the money that has been invested in the system must be protected, and if the tramway line is going to be withdrawn who is going to bear the loss? The authority to operate autobuses is desired in order to give a better service to the people of the city of Quebec. That is all there is in the bill. It will benefit the labour class especially in the constituency of Quebec West and South.
The rates actually in force on the autobuses are the rates agreed to by the tramway contract of 1925. They are not asking for any higher rates for the autobuses. They simply wish to give the people a better service.
Doubt has been expressed whether the language of the act covered autobuses. When I presented the bill I told the house that as far as I was concerned I had no doubt that autobuses were covered by the language of the act, that autobuses were a product of modern science and invention, and that the company had the power to use them. Some of the other lawyers objected and contended that autobuses were not covered, and it was thought better therefore to clarify the language It was felt that it was such a small amendment that there could not possibly be any objection to it.
After all, we are just asking that the language be amended to cover autobuses, a product of modern science and invention. One might just as well call them tramways propelled by gasoline motors, but somebody happened to call them autobuses. What difference does the name make? The main thing is that this bill has been brought before the house to settle all doubts about the matter. The bill confers no exclusive power upon the company, nor does it give them the right to increase their rates or charge any kind of rate, as has been suggested. They are bound by their contract of 1925 with the city of Quebec, and we are not asking the parliament of Canada to do anything about the rates. We are just asking that the original charter,
which was granted at a time when autobuses were not in existence or even thought of, be amended by adding the word "autobuses," in order to remove any doubt that may exist in anybody's mind.
There is nothing in the bill that I can see to prevent any company from being formed by anyone, even by my hon. friend from Temiscouata, to operate autobuses. In fact, I am told that there are already requests before the public utilities commission of Quebec to operate autobuses in competition with this company, and if the public utilities commission grants that power there will be the competition that my hon. friend desires.
To sum up, I say that we are as much in need of autobuses in the city of Quebec as my hon. friend from Temiscouata was in need of a railway station in Riviere du Loup.

Mr. Chairman, if the matter were as serious as suggested by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), I think every member of the house would agree with him. But it is somewhat different. The question was studied in the standing committee on railways and canals, and I should like to explain to the house in a very few words the question that arises.
The Quebec Railway is a corporation incorporated by a statute of the dominion parliament. Therefore the Quebec Railway must seek in its charter, which is chapter 59 of the statutes of 1895, 58 and 59 Victoria, all its powers and authority. A statutory corporation does not possess any other authority than that which is conferred upon it by statute.
Since 1915 the world has continued to move and a great many things have been improved upon, in Quebec as elsewhere, because there is some progress being made from time to time even in Quebec.

subtopic: QUEBEC RAILWAY, LIGHT AND POWER COMPANY
speechtext:
In Quebec it has come about that autobuses are desired on certain streets and in the suburbs. In the city of Montreal, autobuses have replaced street-cars in certain
districts. The city council have directed the Quebec Railway to substitute autobuses for street-cars.
We are not concerned at all with the contracts which were entered into between the Quebec Railway and the city of Quebec. This is not within our jurisdiction. The question arising out of the bill which is before this committee is not that at all. The chairman of the board of transport has expressed a certain doubt as to the power of the Quebec Railway Company to operate buses, and as
1414	COMMONS
Quebec Railway, Light and Power
regards the jurisdiction of the board of transport with respect to buses. Section 2, subsection 21 of the Railway Act, defines a railway. The word "autobuses" is not included. Therefore it was deemed advisable for the Quebec Railway Company to come to parliament to seek authority to operate buses. The committee is not asked to determine the contracts or the privileges or the exclusive franchises of the city of Quebec, in connection with buses. This is not within our jurisdiction, and parliament and this committee are not asked to determine that point. Parliament is asked only to grant to the Quebec Railway Company authority to operate buses if the city of Quebec in its wisdom desires to substitute buses for street cars.
My learned friend, the hon. member for Temiscouata suggested that there was an amphibious jurisdiction. This must be the offspring of his fertile imagination. There is no jurisdiction. Parliament has created a corporation. In any statutory corporation there must be distinguished the authority and the power. Authority and power are not the same thing. I have the authority to buy any real estate in Montreal, but I may not have the purchasing power to buy it. I am entitled to buy it if I like, but I may not have the power. When parliament created the Quebec Railway it gave it the authority to operate but it did not give it the power. Section 10, subsection 4 of the act, stated:
No power or authority granted or authorized under the provisions of this section shall be exercised within the limits of the jurisdiction of the city of Quebec, the Quebec north shore turnpike trustees or any municipality respectively, except with the prior consent in each and every case of such city, trustees or municipality respectively, and upon such conditions as they may severally consent to and agree upon.
Therefore there is no exclusive power. There is only the constitution or creation of a corporation with the authority to operate provided they get power from the municipal authority. So to-night we are not called upon to determine whether there will be exclusive jurisdiction or exclusive power or exclusive privilege and franchise; we are simply called upon to give the authority to the Quebec Railway to operate autobuses or other buses-trolley buses-if the city of Quebec desires to have buses in lieu of the street railway.
I should like to draw the attention of the committee to this point. In committee we added to the end of section 1 the following words:
Subject to all provincial and municipal enactments in respect to highways and motor vehicles operated thereon, and applicable thereto.

Therefore no jurisdiction on the highways is being affected by this bill. If they operate autobuses they will be subject to the public utilities commission of the province of Quebec, and their rates will be subject to the regulations of that body. Moreover, provision is made in the bill as amended to make sure that there is no encroachment on provincial jurisdiction.

speechtext:
I say yes. By this amendment we are conferring a new motor-bus and motor-truck franchise upon this company. The company started as a provincial concern away back in 1895 when it went to the provincial legislature of Quebec and got a charter and an act passed. The incorporation of this company has been declared in eight acts not to be a work for the general advantage of Canada but a purely provincial undertaking. What do we propose to do to-night under this bill? The bill has not been submitted to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, or to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe), nor has he laid down in the house yet the policy of the government with regard to it. We are simply going to create another franchise over the head of the province of Quebec and over the heads of the many other municipalities in that province where the company operates, because the operations of this company are not confined to the city of Quebec alone. The company operates outside the city in the several municipalities which are set out in three or four pages of the statute of 1895. There is no mention of motor-buses in it.
In 1917 the municipalities had a hard fight in the House of Commons when the general Railway Act was being revised. That fight was for the municipal control of streets throughout Canada. A large number of companies had been coming to this parliament and getting statutes passed, and in that year there was a long fight for the municipal control of streets. I had to be down here to 71492-90
protect our streets from new federal franchises. Now that basic principle is involved in this bill-the principle won in 1917 after a long fight that no company may operate on the streets of Canadian municipalities in, on, along, over or under a highway without the consent of the municipality, yet if we pasf this amendment this company may do so over provincial and municipal rights which are in jeopardy.	.
In connection with this bill, section 8 of chapter 59 of the statutes of 1895 does not give the company any such powers as they claim. We are told that the purpose of this bill is to clarify section 8, but I submit that a careful reading of the statute of 1895 will refute this contention. A large number of other sections of that statute must be read in conjunction with section 8 and the whole act, and marginal notes as well, to get the intention of the statute. Does this parliament propose to confer charters on purely provincial and municipal undertakings to allow the operation of motor-buses, taxicabs and so on by special federal enactment. If the national railways had been more active a few years ago, there would be no necessity for a bill such as this, and that railway would have got a bus franchise.
This bill confers a new franchise, and various provincial rights have to be considered. The Toronto transportation commission operates motor-buses in all parts of Ontario and gives a provincial service. It operates under provincial charter, using motor-buses, motor-trucks and some taxis with international affiliations and interprovincial services; it had to buy out competition. What would be the position of that concern if this parliament passed the amendment now submitted to us? To give this company an amendment would be, I repeat, simply to override the municipalities in whose territory the company would operate and give this company exclusive jurisdiction. The company would have the whole area forever for the operation of motor-buses for itself, a franchise without consideration by legislation.
This section is supposed to clarify section 8 in order to resolve doubts as to the company's powers to own and operate the necessary autobuses, trolley buses, and so on. But they have no such power by the original charter. No court of law has declared that they have that power and they know they have not. Not by the widest interpretation of chapter 59 of the statutes of 1895 can it be contended that they have any such power. But they are trying to go over the heads of the province of Quebec and the municipalities, seeking a new form of bus franchise



Quebec Railway, Light and Power
from this high court of parliament. If we pass this amendment the transport commission of Canada will have no control over their rates. Moreover, the amendment would have the effect of giving the company radial entrances not only into the city of Quebec but also into other municipalities for motor-buses, trucks and taxicabs and power, light and buses without municipal consent. It would give the company that whole territory, without affording the municipalities any chance whatsoever to be heard before our committees or the Department of Transport.
Is it any wonder that there is an agitation in the country and that people everywhere are wondering what we are doing in this parliament when we flout the municipalities and the provinces in this manner by conferring new charters on such companies; for that is what it amounts to? I repeat, this amendment to section 8 is not a clarification but a new declaration, the conferring of an absolutely new franchise upon the company to operate in and outside the city of Quebec.
It will be seen in the explanatory note that the object of the amendment is to ensure the company's right to provide transportation "in and in the neighbourhood of the city of Quebec," and the purport of these words is set out in eight or nine pages of the parent statute. If they are to have the right to operate motor-buses they should go to the provincial legislature, which has control over highways in that province, for a new franchise. The province built the highways, and yet an effort is being made in this house to allow this company to use the provincial highways of Quebec without any reference to the provincial legislature or the municipalities who have to license these buses.
The bill is objectionable for another reason. What is the purpose of the railway committee but to consider the principle of bills of this description. In my opinion the bill is a gross infringement of provincial and municipal rights. Has the province of Quebec been asked to make representations with regard to this bill, or have the city of Quebec or the other municipalities who are vitally interested made any representations in the matter? Have they been consulted?

speechtext:
Before the house took recess at six o'clock, I had been discussing the effect of the Canada-United States trade agreement and the concessions made by Canada under the United Kingdom-Canada agreement on the lumber industry in British Columbia, which, as I had pointed out, is the greatest industry in our province. I had shown how the empire agreements of 1932 had been benefiting this lumber industry, and I think the situation with regard to these empire agreements was very well summed up by a noted old country man who visited British Columbia last summer at the head of a delegation from the British lumber trade. He was quoted in the Vancouver Province of August 30 as follows:
Warning against any change in the present British tariff preference on British Columbia lumber was uttered here to-day by E. P. Tetsall, leader of the British lumber delegation which was banqueted by the provincial government at the Empress hotel.
Praising the present tariff arrangement which has built Canadian export to Britain, Mr. Tetsall added: "I should regard it as reactionary and a retrograde step if any change were to take place in the conditions under which the trade has grown up and has prospered."
We now come back to the first stage of the lumber bargain with the United States, which came into effect on January 1 of this year. In this first stage Canada plays fairy godmother to the United States in several ways. In the first place, on about one-fifth of the lumber business which the British Columbia industry has built up with the United Kingdom as a result of the empire trade agreements of 1932-which one-fifth, incidentally, is worth several million dollars to British Columbia-this government gives up about three-fifths of the Canadian preference. That means, in the first place, the loss of some of our business to the United States and, in the second place, more highly competitive prices on the business we do not lose. The loss goes right back to the logger and mill worker in British Columbia. Just within the last week or two, wages in many of our leading mills were cut by ten per cent, and we find the logging business down. Then, in reference to the lumber market, we find such information as this, from the Vancouver Province of February 20, just eight days ago:
British inquiries have been active except for " clears."

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
And "clears" are the type of lumber on which Canada has now given up part of her preference.
The second way in which we have been a fairy godmother to the United States is this: On the whole of our lumber business with the West Indies, which has been built up as a result of the empire agreements, involving about fourteen million feet, the preference has been cut from ten per cent to about four per cent. In the third place our business with Australia, New Zealand and South Africa is affected. These dominions were not parties to the recent tripartite negotiations in Washington, and they have yet to make their terms with the United States. Nevertheless the Canadian government has agreed in advance that no objection will be made to Australia, New Zealand and South Africa cutting our preference to the same extent that it has been cut in the British market. I would refer the house to the lumber declaration, which is a schedule to the treaty, found on page 51. I quote:
-the government of Canada will interpose no objection to the reduction by empire governments other than the United Kingdom-
As I have said, that refers to Australia, New Zealand and South Africa.
*-of differential duties now levied on United States lumber to a point at which the margin of preference enjoyed by Canadian lumber will not exceed the duties and taxes now imposed on Canadian lumber on importation into the United States-
As the fourth gift to the United States, Canada agrees to cut her duty on dressed lumber coming from the United States by one-half, to ten per cent, and to keep United States rough lumber on the free list, with no quota in either case. We also agree to remove the three per cent excise tax. That adds up simply to this, that we are giving the United States a part of British Columbia's market for lumber in the prairie provinces.
In return for these gifts to the United States, in the first stage of the lumber bargain that country graciously agrees, in the first place, to remove the quota of 250,000,000 feet a year imposed on Douglas fir and western hemlock. That is the quota which Canada has never yet been able to fill. Just what value lies in that concession can be best explained by reading from an analysis of this treaty by Senator Lewis B. Schwellenbach, who is United States senator from the state of Washington. His analysis will be found in the Timber Worker, published in Seattle, under date of December 10. 1938. With regard to the removal of the quota he has this to say:
When, with all the public construction going on during the last two and one-half years, the 71402-00J
Canadians never exceeded sixty per cent of their quota, the question of the removal of that ceiling is conclusively proved to be immaterial. Any fair-minded person must agree that in this regard no concession was made by our government.
We find a similar statement at page 51 of the United States press release on the agreement with Canada. Dealing again with the quota the United States government said:
The quota fixed in the 1936 agreement on Douglas fir and western hemlock, although representing a relatively small fraction of the domestic consumption, has not been reached by actual imports, which at their maximum, in 1937, were barely sixty per cent of the quota. This was one of the reasons for dropping the quota provision in the new agreement.
