As the second so-called concession which the United States makes to Canada in the first stage of this lumber bargain, she has agreed to do away with the provision which required Canadian lumber to be marked " made in Canada." This marking provision was a joker put into the United States law by this same Senator Schwellenbach, in the spring of 1938; and I would remind hon. members that this government actually started to negotiate this new treaty away back in 1937. The marking provision came into force in the fall of 1938, just before negotiations were completed. An explanation of that measure will be found at page 400 of the Commercial Intelligence Journal of September 3, 1938, which points out that the law empowered the secretary of the treasury of the United States to except from the marking regulation any imported article, including lumber, subject to a proviso which apparently was put into the United States law by Senator Schwellenbach in the spring of 1938, that such power would not apply after September 1, 1938, to sawed lumber and timber, et cetera, but with this further provision:
-but the president is authorized to suspend the effectiveness of this proviso if he finds such action required to carry out any trade agreement entered into under the authority of the act of June 12, 1934, as extended.
The senator explains it all as follows:
I put this provision into the law. The house committee had refused to accept it, the house

of representatives had refused to adopt it the senate committee had refused to accept it,' and I offered it upon the floor of the United States senate. I finally prevailed upon Senator Walsh of Massachusetts, chairman of the committee to take it to conference. Those who criticized' the treaty know that he succeeded in getting it accepted by the conference only upon the understanding that it probably would be removed through the medium of a treaty.
In other words, it was put in there simply for the purpose of negotiating a treaty. He sums up the value of these so-called concessions that have been given to Canada in the first stage of the lumber bargain as follows:
In the preceding two paragraphs I have outlined in full all the concessions that were granted to the Canadians so far as the lumber industry is concerned. Any honest and fair-minded individual must admit that they amount to nothing.
I think it may fairly foe said that under the first stage of the lumber bargain Canada does all the giving and none of the taking. And this first stage continues in force for the life of the agreement; in other words, it is in force for three years, unless the United States congress chooses to bring the second stage into effect, by dropping the import excise tax of $1.50 a thousand. This excise tax was imposed under the Revenue Act of 1932 for a period of one year, and was renewed for periods of two years each in 1933, 1935 and 1937, so it expires at the end of June of this year. For this possible concession, which is the only one the United States makes in the second stage of the lumber bargain-and which would still leave our lumber subject to a duty of fifty cents a thousand, whereas from 1913 to 1930 it went in free-the British Columbia lumberman, logger, mill worker and employee in the dependent industries pay an added price. First of all, on the one-fifth of our lumber business with the United Kingdom, on which the Canadian preference is now cut by three-fifths, we give up the preference entirely. In other words, we let the other two-fifths go. And we also give it up entirely on a further one-fifth. This means that Canada loses her preference completely on about two-fifths of our lumber business with the United Kingdom.
In the next place, on the whole of our lumber business with the West Indies we give up the preference completely.

Mr. Speaker, I had intended speaking at length in this debate in connection with the trade treaty; but after listening to the speeches delivered during the past ten days in this house, I have decided to change my tactics and I shall content myself with making only a few remarks. I believe almost every angle of this trade treaty has been covered, and any further speeches could hardly help but be repetitious.
The question of trade vitally affects Canada, and rightly so. Listening to the speeches in the house, I am firmly convinced that we all believe in trade and trade treaties. Treaties must always be made on the principle of give and take; some concessions must be granted as well as benefits received. But it must be admitted that Canada has achieved an enviable position, because we are now in fourth position among the exporting nations of the world. No one can deny that prosperity is built on trade, both internal and external, and the more business each country
1420	COMMONS
Canada-United. States Trade Agreement
does, the better it will be for everyone. Many extravagant statements have been made both for and against the treaty, but I cannot see any benefit in discussing this matter any further. Time alone will tell of its merits and demerits. There has been the usual taking of sides in this debate, with parties lining up solidly either for or against the treaty. It seems strange to me that the members of one party should all oppose the treaty, while the members of another party should all be in favour. In order to prove their points they have quoted from certain newspapers. Many United States newspapers have been quoted during the debate. Those papers which were anti-government have contended that the farmers of the United States have been sold down the river, but other newspapers take the opposite view and say that the United States is going to get into the Canadian market. I contend that these references do not mean anything.
The average citizen is not particularly interested in political speeches, but he will be elated if these trade treaties bring more prosperity. I am satisfied that the government have made a comprehensive study of the probable results of this trade treaty. The three men who represented Canada in connection with negotiating this trade treaty were the best qualified men we have. I do not subscribe to the contention of the opposition that Americans are such good traders that Canada was bound to get the worst of the deal. Surely a bargain to the mutual advantage of both countries was possible.
I should like to give a brief history of the three men who carried out the negotiations for this trade treaty. Mr. H. B. McKinnon, commissioner of tariffs, was appointed to the tariff board in 1926. He was one of the officials who took part in the economic conference held at Ottawa in 1932, when the first Canadian-United Kingdom treaty was negotiated. Mr. L. D. Wilgress has been with the Department of Trade and Commerce since 1914. He has represented Canada as a trade commissioner at various points in Europe, including some years in Russia and Germany. Mr. Norman Robertson, first secretary in the Department of External Affairs, was appointed to that department in 1929. These gentlemen took part in the economic conference at Ottawa in 1932, at which time the first United Kingdom-Canada treaty was negotiated.
When the first Canada-United States trade treaty was negotiated in 1935, these three gentlemen represented Canada at Washington They were sent to England in 1936 when the United Kingdom trade agreement was revised, and they were again Canada's representatives at the negotiation of the trade treaty we are now discussing in the house. These gentlemen were ten months in Washington negotiating this trade treaty. They were in daily communication with the ministers at Ottawa and had at their disposal all the information available in the departments. They were quite able to judge the benefits or disadvantages of the treaty. It is quite true, as was stated this afternoon by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth), that these men were sent by this government to negotiate the agreement. However, from what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) says, I am satisfied that no legitimate business in Canada will be injured by this treaty. Markets for our primary products are of great consideration to a country like Canada, with only about 11,000,000 people and yet possessing vast natural resources. If these treaties give us a wider market for our lumber, fish, pulp, potatoes, minerals, live stock and dairy products, and they will, then our secondary industries also will profit, as will Canada as a whole.
If I recall correctly the remarks of the hon. member for Waterloo South, he stated that no one had spoken for the industrial worker of this country. I do not think that is a fair statement to make. I think every Canadian is interested in the industrial workers of this country, but we cannot get away from the fact that the primary producer produces and the rest of the people derive their livelihood by exchanging their goods and services for the products of the primary producer. Until the primary producer is in a prosperous state, we cannot expect to have economic prosperity in Canada.
These treaties are already in operation, and there can be no further point in discussing them in this house. I cannot see the value of some of the speeches that have been delivered during this debate. This afternoon the hon. member for Waterloo South said that this government was living in the past. I am not so sure of that. I can recall a speech delivered this week by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), and if he did not go back into the hoary past, then I do not know who did. I cannot remember back to the point at which he first started; for I do not believe I was born then, but when his forty minutes were up he was at least eight years away from the date of the trade treaty under discussion. I well recall the cry against the reciprocity pact in 1911. At that time the slogan was: "No truck or trade with the Yankees." Again in 1936 many people saw ruin and desolation because of the trade agreement which had

Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
been negotiated. I can well recall, when the $100 exemption was under discussion in this house, how the members of the opposition painted a picture of Canadians going into the United States and bringing back so many goods that all the border industries would be ruined. I looked into this matter along the St. Clair river in December, 1937, and I found that- very few people brought back the full $100 worth of exemptions.
It is the same old cry of ruin and desolation that is being raised. We all remember the story of the boy who cried "wolf" when there was no wolf. Such a cry may appeal for a while, but I feel sure the Canadian people will not be unduly alarmed about the story of the terrible ruination that is going to come upon the country. It is true we criticize each other, and probably we always shall, but at heart we want the same things. We want to preserve our freedom and liberty, not only for ourselves and for our children, but for our children's children. These trade pacts have the tendency to bring democratic countries closer together as trading units. I was greatly interested in the remarks of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) when he spoke in Essex the other day. He said that this parliament had been in session for six weeks, and he wanted to know what the government had done.

The treaty is in operation and we cannot change it. Why prolong this debate any further? If freedom of speech is one of the bulwarks of democracy, let us not play it to death in this House of Commons. I think we shall have to change our tactics if this House of Commons is to continue under our present constitution. I am quite convinced, and I am sure that other hon. members are likewise convinced, that at least half the business of the country could have been done by this time if we had not wanted to make political speeches in this House of Commons.
I am not going to be a sinner in that respect myself. We cannot change the trade pacts, so why debate the subject any longer? That is the attitude I take.

The $100 exemption does, and that is what they are all working on. Many people do not declare what they have bought. They say " What is the use of declaring? I haven't a hundred dollars' worth." When the minister was questioned with reference to shoes, he said some compensation might be given to shoe manufacturers by lowering the duties on some of their raw products. That is the vicious circle which runs through this whole business. This government has put one manufacturer against another. They lower the duty on one product; the person who is affected by the lower duty comes here and asks for a further concession, and so it has gone on all over Canada. The whole manufacturing fabric of this country to-day is, as was said this afternoon, jittery. They do not know what to do. If there were an election in progress I have no doubt they would say a great deal, but they are too scared and panicky as to what may be done in the course of the budget. After that is over, I imagine that these gentlemen will start to talk a great deal.
There are many things I could say about the furniture problem. Somebody referred to it this afternoon re these duties. The furniture manufacturers are told, "we are going to let machinery in for a little less duty, but there may be a reduction on your paints and one thing and another"-the same vicious circle. I protest against it just as strongly as I can. It is attacking one manufacturer through another, and by attacking one manufacturer after another, driving men out of work in the factories which manufacture these lines of materials. For instance, last year $742,000 worth of furniture was imported from the United States. That is equivalent to the labour

of 350 men, I am told. It would look pretty good to have 350 men working in the factories at Kitchener. If they had work for 350 men in Strathroy, it might be possible to re-start the factory which went out of business; or if they could find work for 350 men in the McLagan factory at Stratford which is stopped, it might be started up again.
In addition to the importation of $742,000 worth of furniture last year, a considerable amount-it is hardly distinguishable how much -came in under the $100 exemption. Furniture, I notice, is linked up with household appliances, of which some $756,000 worth entered Canada in eight months; it will probably amount to a million dollars in the twelve months. Probably that would mean the importation of half a million dollars' worth of furniture. A large number of men will have lost their jobs on that account. As I said a moment ago, the government proposes to try to fix matters up by lowering duties on other lines, and here, too, we have a vicious circle. One form of production after another is attacked from one end of the country to the other. Is it any wonder that we have unemployment in Toronto and other centres? Just wait until the weather improves, and I have no doubt that the unemployment parade which will come to this city of Ottawa will stagger everyone and will outdo anything that has ever occurred in that line.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) gave four reasons for supporting this treaty. I shall not mention them all. The first is, that it is to facilitate rather than to obstruct the making of the agreement between the United Kingdom and the United States. The next two reasons are along the same lines; the fourth one does not say anything about labour, either. I would say that when the government makes a treaty, the thing it should keep before it above anything else is what that treaty will mean in the matter of unemployment in this country. The government has not done that. That is one thing it has entirely forgotten. In by far the majority of cases the provisions of the treaty will affect the labour market from one end of the dominion to the other. The Minister of National Revenue also said that we are not directly affected by Great Britain's protectionism to any more than a small extent because she lets most of our products into her markets free of duty. He might have added that now she is going to let United States wheat into her markets free of duty. This country gets it from every angle and gets the wrong end of the angle every time.
When the Minister of National Revenue was speaking on February 21, something was said about apples. On Saturday last I over-

heard an interesting conversation on this subject. The minister said that he had no complaints from his province, Nova Scotia, with reference to the tariff on apples. At that time he did have complaints. Last Saturday I came down in an elevator in a Toronto building with two gentlemen, one of whom knew me. He called me by name, and then he said, "we were just discussing the tariff schedules in connection with apples. This gentleman," he said, "comes from Nova Scotia and is an apple packer." I said, "Don't give me his name because I might be asked in the House of Commons what it is." Not having his name I cannot give it. He told me, however, that representations had been made to the government, and on that date the minister must have known all about the representations. I assume he did know because in his speech he makes a statement with reference to compensation. He does not use that word and perhaps I had better read what he says:
. . . on some of their supplies, particularly on spraying and dusting materials and fertilizers, and upon agricultural implements, including spraying and other orcharding machinery from which the 3 per cent special excise tax is to be removed.
He intimates that the apple producer will receive some concession, and I say again that we have the same vicious circle. You attack one producer and in trying to compensate him you attack another; that is why from one end of the country to the other employment is diminishing all the time.
I wish to discuss for a moment the remarks of the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean), because I interrupted him when he referred to the policy adopted by the Conservative party at its convention. At page 1208 of Hansard he is reported as having said:
_ When the Conservative convention was held in Ottawa and the new leader was chosen, they adopted a resolution stating that the party stands by its old principle of high protection.
I interjected that it was not so, and I think it would be in order to read the policy of the Conservative party in connection with protection, as adopted at the national convention :
This national Conservative convention declares its continued adherence to its traditional policy of fostering and sustaining by fiscal protection Canadian labour and Canadian industries, and especially the primary industries of agriculture, fisheries, forestry and mining, all of which are essential to the maintenance of a well-balanced national economy, while, at the same time, guarding against undue advantage being taken of the protection so afforded.
That was one means of protection that the last Conservative government took in connection with the tariff. They did not write

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
it on the basis that the height of the tariff was the whole concern; but the object was to prevent the exploitation of the consumer, and therefore they made agreements with the manufacturers not to enhance prices if they were given an opportunity to manufacture in this country. In my opinion that principle should be embodied in any tariff policy adopted in this country. It goes on:
It also affirms its adherence to the underlying principles of that policy, which have served to stimulate the development of the natural resources of Canada, to preserve and to enlarge the domestic markets for Canadian products, to promote interprovincial trade, and, generally, to provide a diversified economic life which will serve to retain Canada's sons and daughters within our own boundaries.
That is one of the bases of the Conservative party's policy, whereas one of the results of the trade treaties which this government has now negotiated has been to cause unemployment in very large measure, and the unemployed remain in Canada only because they cannot enter the United States.
This convention affirms the policy of having tariff schedules under scientific investigation by a permanent tariff commission and that, in case it is ascertained that unfair advantage is being taken of any customs duties imposed by such schedules, the tariff commission shall make recommendations, to which effect shall be given by the government, for reducing such rates of duty or for removing them from the tariff schedules.
This convention affirms its firm adherence to the policy of preferential trade within the British commonwealth of nations, by which Canada obtained the boon of tariff preferences in the markets of the United Kingdom and of other dominions, and which have served to mitigate the severity of the trade depression during recent years, and which -were approved by parliament, despite the bitter, determined and prolonged opposition of the Liberal party.
This convention is convinced that the permanent interests of Canada are best conserved by enlarging our markets-
I have heard someone say that we do not want markets. Our platform says:
-by enlarging our markets in the United Kingdom and other British dominions, whose products are more complementary than competitive with those of this country, and with which our trade agreements are more likely to be durable and beneficial.
This convention believes that the external trade of Canada may also be increased advantageously by the negotiation on a fair and equitable basis

That is what we say the present treaty does not do. It is not fair to Canada, certainly not to the Canadian manufacturer and the Canadian workmen in the factory.
-of trade agreements with countries which are outside of the British empire, but that in negotiations with foreign countries, the _ terms agreed upon should not be such as to impair the benefits derived by Canada under existing
agreements between Canada and the United Kingdom and between Canada and other British dominions.

speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit me to ask a question?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES'-CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
My time is passing
rapidly; no doubt hon. members opposite would like to take up some of it, but I must hurry on. All along the line this treaty is going to bring about reductions in employment. Within the last few days I spoke to a gentleman who in 1932 had four hundred men employed in his plant. As a result of the 1935 treaty that number was cut down, and now he foresees nothing but the closing of his plant. His employees have been reduced to some 275. I believe, and he expects that within a reasonable length of time he will close the plant entirely and buy from the parent plant in the United States what he requires for the Canadian market. Any treaty that will close up a plant-and this is only one of scores and scores of plants-and throw the employees on the labour market is, in my judgment, certainly not a good treaty.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES'-CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: Time.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES'-CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
No, my time is not up
yet. Some speakers have referred to the press release issued by the United States government in connection with the present treaty, before it went into operation. I should like to quote a little from the press release issued by the United States government after the 1935 treaty was in operation, in which they say:
These trade increases were widely distributed among many classes of American producers, and were most notable in . . . cotton and rayon piece goods and wearing apparel; furniture; periodicals, advertising pamphlets and printed matter and various paper products; automotive products, including tractors; radios, refrigerators and other elrotrical apparatus; electroplated ware; a wide range of machinery and implements, agricultural and industrial; and in metal products generally.
I have been associated with the metal industry for a long time, and this is one thing that gives me a great deal of concern. I want to laugh when someone on the opposite side talks about the increase in our exports of industrial products to the United States. In 1938 our exports of iron products of all kinds to the United States amounted to $4,000,000, while our imports of the same kind of materials amounted to $134,000,000. It is not of much assistance to the iron industry of Canada to enact tariffs that reduce employment in practically every iron industry in Canada and which at the same time increase employment in United States factories to the extent to which a favourable balance of $130,000,000 will provide employment over there. Much of that money should have been spent in this country to furnish employment here.
I think I have time to refer just a little further to the results of the trade treaty. What is to be charged up to your former trade treaty? Your former trade treaty had thrown many thousands of men out of work. Your new trade treaty will throw thousands more in industry out of work. In that way you reduce the market for the primary producer.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES'-CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: And hit the farmer, as well.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES'-CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
What does the press say about employment in Canada, as a result of this government's tariff tinkering? I shall read only the headings, because I have not time for more. The first reads: "Youth urged to demand jobs from government." Youth will never get them from the present government, when its actions are resulting in throwing multitudes out of work.
And the next: "Youth unemployment is termed emergency by Brantford rally." Of course. And the present tariff will affect many more in Brantford.
And the next:	"Youths' gaoling called
terrible." Of course. The gaols are half full of youths who would never be there if they could get enough to do. How can they get anything to do when the factories from one end of Canada to the other are closing?
And the next: "Service clubs join in task. Joint committee is formed to seek immediate steps by government to meet unemployment problem." They have a fat chance of having this government do anything in connection with the unemployment problem.
And the next: "Relief cost shows jump-"

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I listened to the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen) and heard him make the statement that social credit was not doing so well in Alberta. May I suggest to the hon. member that it is the Liberal party that is not doing so well in Alberta, and that there had been a greater reduction in unemployment in Alberta than there has been in the province from which the hon. member comes. There has been more money invested in industry and in building in Alberta than has been invested or spent in building or in construction in the hon. member's province.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES'-CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext: What kind of money?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES'-CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
And not only that, but the cash position of Alberta is better than that of the province from which the hon. member for Marquette comes.
Many references have been made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and other members of the government to the success of the Liberal party in the elections of 1935, and to their success in the by-elections which have taken place since that time. But may I remind the Prime Minister and his government that their success has been very much limited in Alberta, both in the general election and in the by-elections which have taken place since. We can recall the by-election which took place in Edmonton East, where it was impossible for three cabinet ministers to put on sufficient pressure to defeat the hon. member who now represents that constituency in the house, and is attached to the party to which I belong. As a sage of old said, "That which is not good will not last." The Liberal party is through in Alberta.

They have read, no doubt, of the last of the Mohicans. Well, we now have the last of the Liberals in the person of the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. MacKinnon), who has been honoured by his party, and rightly so. I say that because of all the Liberals who ran for office in Alberta he was one of the fortunate ones who saved his deposit. So I do not think much satisfaction can be derived from the success of the Liberal party in Alberta.
Of course, the Conservatives did not fare so well either-but they did just as well as the Liberals. At that time there was one Conservative returned to the house.

There is still a
remnant of the Conservative party left in Alberta, but they are trying to join up with the remnant of the Liberal party to form some sort of unity league. I believe the Liberals and Conservatives should unite federally, because they have this in common at least: They are both determined to take no fundamental step to change existing conditions in Canada. They are both satisfied to sit and do nothing. Neither one of them is prepared to make the far-reaching changes which are so essential to get us out of the financial mess in which we find ourseives.

Before dealing with the observations of the Prime Minister, I believe I should refer to a statement made by the hon. member for Marquette in regard to the application of social credit principles to dominion affairs. He felt we should wait until such time as the whole world would adopt those principles. May I remind the Liberal party that they still advocate free trade, and yet the whole world does not seem to have adopted it. And, as an hon. member to my right suggests, neither does the Liberal party. I believe the record will bear me out. That is exactly the position taken by the Liberals in regard to our movement. They suggest that nothing can be done provincially or federally, that we must wait until the whole world accepts social credit. All we are suggesting is that we should abolish poverty in the midst of plenty, but they say to us: "Do not attempt to abolish poverty in the midst of plenty until the Chinese have taken the same steps, until poverty has been abolished in India, Africa and Afghanistan." They tell us not
to establish just prices until the whole world has done so. What sort of reasoning is that? Let me read what the originator of this great movement once said, speaking from the world point of view. Major Douglas was asked this question:
Since under the Canadian constitution control over banking, finance, trade and commerce rests entirely with the dominion government, is it not desirable that advocates of social credit centre their main efforts upon the dominion rather than the provincial field?

speechtext: I have sat in the house and listened to addresses made by hon. members on both sides, and I have heard them fight out every election since 1911 and discuss every subject from soup to nuts; yet I am prevented, as I understand it, from answering the points raised by the hon. member.

The Prime Minister

He declared that it was the fulfilment of all the promises made by the Liberal party in regard to trade before the election of 1935. I recall the Prime Minister and other members of the Liberal party declaring that their promises in regard to monetary reform had been fulfilled, and then shortly afterwards bringing in an amendment to the Bank of Canada Act. Those were strange proceedings. If the people of Canada do not receive any more benefits from the fulfilment of the promises of the Liberal party with regard to trade than they did from the fulfilment of the promises of the Liberal party in regard to monetary reform, then God help the people of Canada.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES'-CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON MOTION FOR APPROVAL SUBJECT TO REQUIRED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
We say that the
prosperity of Canada should not depend upon the height of a tariff wall. Our prosperity should depend less and less upon foreign trade. If we depend too much upon foreign trade for our prosperity we are likely

to become involved in national and international complications which will create problems and hard feelings at home which may eventually lead to war abroad. Why should we bring dairy products and wool from New Zealand into this country in exchange for automobiles, when our farmers have to walk and when we keep on producing a surplus of dairy products and wool?
The Prime Minister declared that the nations of the world are endeavouring to practise what he termed economic nationalism, that they were trying to get into isolated compartments. We have never suggested that, and I challenge the government to name one nation that has stated their policy to be one of economic nationalism, which means virtual isolation as far as trade is concerned.	I ask them to name one nation
which has refused to trade with the world.
I know that after the revolution many countries refused to trade with Russia and enforced economic nationalism upon that country, but what country of any importance has declared to-day that it refuses to trade with other nations of the world?
I listened to the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) state that Italy and Germany did not want to trade with the nations of the world. I suggest that he read something in addition to the speeches of his leader. Just the other day Germany stated that she must trade to live, and England replied that she must trade or die. We hear that Germany wants to trade $30,000,000 worth of machinery for $30,000,000 worth of wheat and other commodities. How can anyone say that we as a party, that the Conservatives as a party, or that the people of any nation as a nation refuse to trade? Why should they condemn social crediters or others who advocate that our own people should be supplied from our own natural resources? We want to utilize our natural resources for our own people. Why try to blast our way into foreign markets when we cannot get into our own?

speechtext: My hon. friend says, " Why not twenty-five dollars a month?" I agree with him, and I ask him, why not? And he cannot answer me, or at any rate he has failed to answer me. If my hon. friend will be patient, I shall deal with that point. I remember that just the other day the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) agreed with me when I said that the most urgent problem in Canada to-day was the need of increased purchasing power to the consumer. I believe that even the Liberal party would agree to that. I have no doubt that my Cooperative Commonwealth Federation friends would also do so. So we find general agreement among all hon. members that we must have increased purchasing power for the consumer. But we differ as to the method, and so the people do without, while we argue over the method. I know the Liberal party will never find the way to do it, because they put too much confidence in their theories of world trade. We know they have no solution. The consumer should be financed. There is plenty of money for production. Hon. members have said that we have in Canada an ample amount of money for productive purposes. But I ask them this question, what is the use of investing money in increased production when we cannot buy that which is produced to-day? Factories are working part-time; the goods come out; and what do the retailers do? They sell them at a dollar down and a dollar the next time they can get it.

Progress reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Tomorrow we intend to take up some of the government measures on the order paper. There seem to be quite a number of speakers on the trade treaty, but we are really anxious to do some other work.

I hear that there are
twenty-dwo speakers on the Liberal side, ^till waiting.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, no; unfortunately they are coming from the other side.
No, my hon. friends have more than we have, and rightly so. They have the numbers and they need the defence.

members on this side of the house have been exercising a good deal of restraint.
